records.text: inearity of credit curves (in other words, boxes when the yield of an issuer is compared to that of another issuer with higher perceived creditworthiness at two different maturity points, e.g. 3s10s Italy-Germany) is a well-known feature of credit markets. For low levels of spreads typically associated with investment grade issuers and during economic expansions any pricing of credit deterioration/improvement is concentrated into the future, leading to bear-steepening/bull-flattening dynamics for credit curves. However, at sufficiently wide levels of spreads credit concerns start to be felt disproportionately in shorter maturities. When investors are potentially exposed to meaningful risk of debt restructuring and/or currency re-denomination they are forced to think in price terms rather than yield terms and this will translate very differently across the yield due to the different modified duration and convexity (see Exhibit 1 for an example). For this reason, inversion of the credit curve is considerably more frequent for high yield bonds and during recessions.

This is no longer simply a defensive market hiding from macro risk. The SPI is close to evenly split between cyclical and defensive sectors, Consumer Discretionary led returns last month, and Switzerland has outperformed ACWI defensives since April as well as Europe over the most recent month. That is a meaningful change in market character. The caveat is that the macro handover is not clean. KOF remains below 100, our economists expect growth to run somewhat below trend after the strong Q1 boost, and consumer and labour-market signals are stabilising rather than accelerating. records.Author: Bruna Skarica
records.text: e impact of Brexit on the UK economy remains a subject of debate, from the totality of the data evidence one can deduce that erecting non-tariff barriers to trade with the UK's closest trading partner has adversely impacted the manufacturing sector. Flatlining business investment over the post- referendum, pre-Brexit period likely added to what was already a pressing issue of weak productivity growth post-GFC. All in all, in a decade where the UK economy saw a series of external supply-side shocks – post-pandemic supply-chain disruptions, 2022 natural gas price spike, 2026 oil price spike – Brexit was a domestically-generated supply-side shock that weighed on UK trade and growth. We are less convinced that Brexit has materially altered the nature of the UK labour market, although more evidence over a period without external energy shocks and with a more muted pace of increase in the minimum wage would be needed in order to make that deduction more firmly. That the government has recently introduced various employment rights reforms will complicate this analysis further.

records.text: Japan Macro Watch26 June 2026 ab 3 This cautious approach is understandable. The government's annual economic policy blueprint ("honebuto no hōshin") this year shifts the fiscal policy objective away from achieving a primary balance surplus toward reducing the debt-to-GDP ratio. This change implies that policymakers must pay attention not only to the primary balance, but also to nominal economic growth and interest-rate developments. Even if the primary balance returns to surplus, the debt-to-GDP ratio could still deteriorate if the interest rate is relatively higher than nominal GDP growth (Figure 3). Therefore, securing market confidence and preventing undesirable increases in borrowing costs are prerequisites for pursuing a more expansionary fiscal policy stance. The government is expected to continue communicating cautiously on fiscal matters. Significant uncertainties remain, particularly regarding the funding sources for new policy initiatives, and these issues warrant careful monitoring. Recent announcements have not triggered a noticeable increase in risk premia within the Japanese government bond market. records.text: In essence, the CPI price index will not receive much direct upside pressure despite some of the eye-popping growth rates. To be sure, there are other channels that could see a stronger near- term inflation impulse via electricity, AI-related industrial metals, a consumption boost from the wealth effect, or even tightness in pockets of the labor market, etc. but those are beyond the scope of this note. By contrast, one second-order channel related to computer software and accessories comes via how the Fed chooses to interpret these dynamics, and this may prove to be more consequential for inflation pricing beyond the next few quarters. For instance, if a consensus on the FOMC emerges that the inflationary consequences for PCE should be taken seriously and not dismissed via trimmed measures or some newly-determined "supercore" , this would naturally imply a more restrictive stance of monetary policy, and thus the market should price higher real yields and lower inflation risk, all else equal. Indeed, that is our baseline assumption with Fed policy rates on hold and a hike bias. The reverse is also true in that an attempt to look through the higher core PCE inflation using trimmed measures (or anything else) would imply a lower rate path, and higher CPI-based inflation risk. Even if the market prices the risk in a more top-down fashion, another factor weighing on risks beyond the next few quarters is the sequencing and timing of the supply response to these elevated prices. records.text: M Idea 8 The effective tariff rate, tariff receipts and refunds The tariff rate on US imports has fallen to 8.3% in 1Q26 data On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court struck down the President's authority to impose tariffs under IEEPA. Section 122 tariffs will replace IEEPA tariffs in the short term, though uncertainty rises after the 150-day period when Congress would need to extend those tariffs. Replacing IEEPA with Section 122 tariffs of 15% and considering composition effects of US imports, we estimate baseline tariffs near 11%. Our estimate of "core" tariffs (ex fuels, gold and AI-related imports) remains closer to 13-14%. In our view, near-term tariffs are likely capped below 'Liberation Day' levels, at least until Section 232 and 301 investigations are complete. In the April 2026 data, the effective tariff rate is estimated at ~6.9%, and the 1Q26 tariff rate averages to 8.3%. The latest activity data continue to overstate reacceleration Given our discussions with clients and recent rate developments, one of the key prevailing narratives is that activity and spending are regaining steam in the US, bringing Fed hikes into view. Although we cannot rule out this possibility, this week's estimates seem to lean against that narrative, on the margin. To be sure, the latest headline measures of GDP and spending seem better aligned with the notable pickup in job gains from March-May. The BEA revised up Q1 real GDP growth by 0.5pp to 2.1% q/q saar (Barclays: 2.0% q/q saar; consensus: 1.6% q/q saar), but details indicate that the upgrade was more than accounted for by revisions to the noisy net exports component rather than indications of stronger domestic demand. Finally, the UK's labour supply and participation rate are above what the OBR expected for 2025/26 back in March 2020. This is due to the increase in non-EU migration over 2022, 2023 and 2024. It is hard, we think, to make the argument that Brexit delivered a material hit to labour supply growth. One could instead argue that ending the freedom of movement introduced additional frictions in the UK labour market. EU migrants had the same rights as UK-born workers, whereas non- EU migrants' jobs are linked to their work permits and visas. In practice, it is hard to find solid evidence of meaningful structural changes in the labour market. More evidence is likely needed, but as of now, we would stress two things: I) when the UK labour market tightened in 2022, it was rebalanced – as it had been many times before – by immigration; II) in 2026, as the labour market slack has risen and inflation expectations have cooled, pay growth in the UK has normalised. As noted, we find it hard to identify material structural changes in these developments. So what, then, is the impact of Brexit on the UK economy? As long as the situation in the Middle East stabilizes, we believe uncertainty over the economy should recede, and the BoJ is likely to become even more focused on upside risks to inflation. In recent years, firms have become more accustomed to passing higher costs on to prices, and the BoJ is strongly alert to the possibility that the mechanism through which higher crude oil prices lead to higher inflation has strengthened compared with the past. We therefore expect the BoJ to decide on its next rate hike in October, with a somewhat shorter interval between hikes, followed by a final hike in April 2027. Our forecast for the terminal rate remains 1.5%. However, the rate-hike path could be affected by domestic and overseas political developments. In particular, if BoJ leadership proposes additional rate hikes going forward, we believe dissenting votes are likely to rise to four out of nine by July 2027, assuming PM Takaichi nominates doves to replace the Policy Board members whose terms expire on her watch. In this sense, even if Treasury Secretary Bessent continues to call for further rate hikes, the window in which the BoJ can raise rates may gradually narrow. 26 June 2026 3 Barclays | Market Strategy Japan: Unpacking the JPY370trn public-private investment plan

This divergence creates a policy dilemma. If the Fed focuses too heavily on aggregate consumption and GDP, driven disproportionately by higher-income households, it risks underestimating weakness among lower-income households and maintaining overly restrictive policy. But if it focuses too heavily on pockets of weakness, i.e, lower-income households, it risks easing too aggressively while higher-income demand continues to support activity and keep inflation pressures elevated. In this environment, neither the reflation nor the stagflation narrative fully captures the economy on its own. Also, each has a different policy prescription. Why gradualism remains appropriate Navigating this tension reinforces the case for gradualism rather than aggressive policy moves in either direction when faced with this conundrum. This is in line with the Fed’s recent reaction function where the Fed has moved very cautiously through these data conundrums driven in part by a K-shaped consumer. Importantly, the Fed's dual mandate is framed around maximum employment and price stability rather than GDP growth or consumer spending. As a result, policymakers typically place greater weight on labor market conditions than on measures of aggregate activity when the two diverge. We then analyse the distribution of outstanding bonds by investor type to assess the proportion held by price-insensitive investors, such as domestic cen tral banks. European Revenue Exposure European corporates earn the majority of their revenues abroad, with just 45% generated within Developed Europe. This marks a slight increase compared with last year, following nearly three decades of declining exposure to Developed Europe (Exhibit 12 ). On a free-float market cap weighted basis, the proportion is lower, with just 40% of revenues earned in Developed Europe. By contrast, when looking at domestic exposure by country of domicile, we find that just 22% of European companies' revenues are generated within their home market, which is a further decline vs last year (Exhibit 17 ). North America remains the most important foreign market for European corporates, driving 22% of revenues, closely followed by Asia Pacific at 17%, almost half of which is driven by China. The grey areas denote episodes when the Fed’s policy target was at the zero lower bound (ZLB), which should lower the sensitivity of short -term rates independent of any impact from forward guidance. Th e blue vertical line is drawn in August 2003, when the Fed began to provide forward guidance on the fed funds rate in some form. (Under Greenspan this was qualitative, with language like “measured pace”; over time and especially post-GFC it became much more concrete.) What stands out is that surprises to the current policy target have been substantially smaller since the Fed began using forward guidance. This can be formalized in regressions that show a significant reduction in surprises post - 2003, even after controlling for the ZLB. But beyond the very near term, it’s tough to find any discernible change; eyeballing the right -side chart you would be hard pressed to pick out a guidance-related shift in 2y UST reactions. This is also true for longer maturities (5y, 10y, 30y USTs) and even at horizons as short as the 2nd- quarter-ahead ED/SOFR futures contract. The inference we draw is that , while forward guidance and related communications have steered expectations for meetings towards delivered outcomes, it has not had a big impact in anchoring expectations beyond that. Specifically, Takaichi administration’s “high pressure economy” policies, alongside higher oil prices, have pushed USDJPY via inflation risk premium well above our mid‑140s fair value estimate. At the same time, FX flow dynamics remain negative for JPY, as outbound investment (~JPY40trn) continues to exceed the current account surplus (~JPY20trn), reinforcing sustained net selling pressure. Household portfolio reallocation into foreign assets (including ~JPY10trn annual through NISA) and robust outbound FDI should keep capital outflows elevated. FX interventions are unlikely to shift the trend in USDJPY amid hawkish Fed pricing, while the BoJ is unlikely to accelerate its rate hiking cycle. We see room for some break above 2024- high of 162 in USDJPY due to greater headwinds for the JPY and a failure or perceived unwillingness to intervene risks an even greater upside in USDJPY. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Migration | Rapid rise in non-EU immigration: In the March 2020 Economic and Fiscal Outlook, the OBR projected that net migration flows would decline from 265k per year to 190k per year by 2025. It expected EU migration to fall sharply and to only partly be offset by non-EU migration. However, following the post-pandemic reopening of the UK economy in 2021/22, non-EU migration rose rapidly, with ~1% per annum population expansion recorded between 2022 and 2025. Non-EU migrants look to have largely ended up in employment, with non-EU born workers the only driver of employment growth since 2020. In March 2020, the OBR projected that UK labour supply would be at 34.9 million in 1Q25, whereas in 1Q25, it was 2% higher. The scale of the migration flows was so large, and the inflow of migrant workers into the labour market so fast, that the UK's participation rate in aggregate looks only marginally lower than pre-Covid. It is indeed higher than what the OBR expected in March 2020. This is despite a sharp drop in the participation rate of UK-born workers in the post-Covid period. There is ongoing debate within the MPC around the nature of the UK's post-Brexit labour market. Chief Economist Pill views additional frictions (for example, non-EU migrants cannot change jobs as easily as EU migrants were able to, pre-Brexit) as likely to have caused a structural shift in the labour market, making it more inflationary and less dynamic. records.text: Appendix Investors Intelligence Survey: Created in 1963. The survey is carried out by the investment services provider Investors Intelligence and covers the market views of 130 independent newsletters (brokerage house letters excluded), most of which are published weekly. The list of advisers is reviewed thanks to Barron’s or web searches. The survey reports the findings as the percentage of advisers who are bullish/ bearish/ expect a correction, and is based on the question “are you telling their readers to buy or sell?” The survey is released each Wednesday morning, with most of the opinions written prior to the previous Friday’s market close. AAII Sentiment Survey: Sentiment of individual investors (bullish or bearish) towards the stock market over the next 6 months. The data are weekly since 1987 and are collected by the AAII (The American Association of Individual Investors) via a survey of a subset of their members. Response rates vary, but on average they obtained 315 responses each week from the start of 2013, for example, with the weekly period defined as from Thursday to Wednesday. During this window, AAII members participate by visiting the Sentiment Survey page on AAII.com and voting. The survey is open to all members, although a weekly email is sent to a rotating group of members reminding them to participate. Results are published online early each Thursday morning. Our forecast is consistent with the direction pointed by our equity analysts and dbDIG airfares tracker. Airfares HICP is likely to rise further over the summer, reflecting the gradual pass-through from higher fuel prices over the past three months. We also forecast core goods inflation drifting lower to 0.8% YoY from 0.9% in May. Clothing is likely to account for most of the decline, offsetting continued upside pressures from durable goods (namely IT equipment – Apple announced yesterday it will be raising prices for some of its products by ~20%). This month, the inclusion of additional clothing sales days in France (three more than last year) could add some volatility to the print. We pencil in French clothing HICP at -1.2% MoM vs +0.6% MoM in Jun -25. This, together with some potential payback i n Spain (clothing MoM was unusually strong in March and April only saw a marginal correction), could drive euro area clothing – and core goods – prices temporarily lower (see here for more on the recent stickiness of core goods inflation). The June manufacturing PMI showed some easing in the price balances, but the March increase has not fully reversed. Their still-elevated levels suggest pipeline pressures remain firm and consistent with a further acceleration in goods HICP towards the end of 2026/beginning of 2027 (Figure 4). Against this backdrop, our economists also expect inflation to slow materially on a sequential basis over the second half of the year. The impact of tariffs on core goods inflation has likely peaked, rent inflation should continue to slow for at least the next year, and a number of components should support a slowing in core services ex- housing inflation, including a decline in airfares. We project core PCE inflation to run at 2.0% saar over the last six months of the year, bringing the y/y rate to 3.0% by December (or 3.1% q4/q4), and we see core PCE falling to 2.4% in 2027 (see here). If the data evolve as we expect, we believe the Fed is likely to leave rates on hold over the balance of the year. Despite the hawkish signaling from the shift in the dots in last week’s SEP , the composition of those dots matters. Our economists believe that of the 12 voting members on the FOMC, only three, or perhaps four assumed hikes this year would be appropriate. Meanwhile, though Warsh did not provide much information about his own outlook, he continued to say he believed the adoption of AI would allow for noninflationary growth. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Possibility of FX intervention As noted above, USD/JPY has moved closer to the 161.95 high reached in 2024, and investor questions about another round of FX intervention have started to increase again. From the perspective of the FX level alone, intervention at any time would not be surprising. However, based on recent comments from senior MoF officials, actual intervention still appears some distance away. Finance Minister Katayama has stated that the authorities stand ready to take decisive action at any time if necessary. However, recent remarks have not included language that clearly defines current FX moves as “speculative.” Historically, FX intervention has tended to be implemented after authorities confirm that positions are significantly skewed in one direction and deemed speculative, in order to maximize the effect of intervention (see Exhibit 5 and Exhibit 6 ). records.text: Outlook for the economy and prices (last updated 19 June) In the second preliminary estimate of Q1 GDP released by the Cabinet Office on 8 June, real growth was revised down to 1.8% q/q saar from an initial 2.1%. This was mainly due to capex adjustments (to 2.8% q/q saar from 1.1%), reflecting the findings of the corporate survey. However, as a broad range of other components underwent upward adjustment, the downward revision to real GDP growth was modest relative to market expectations. This strong Q1 result did not fully reflect the impact of Middle East tensions, which intensified from late February onward. Looking ahead, higher energy prices stemming from these developments will weigh on both consumption and capex. If supply constraints in products such as naphtha materialize, the impact could expand in a non-linear manner. That said, assuming tensions in the Middle East will gradually ease, we would expect firms to resume active investment aimed at rebuilding supply chains to cope with labor shortages, while consumption also recovers, supported by large wage hikes. From the H2 FY26 onward, the fiscal policy of the Takaichi administration, which is aiming for a high-pressure economy, is also expected to provide some support for growth. On the price front, core-core inflation (CPI excluding perishables and energy) eased slightly in May, but looking ahead we expect the impact of higher oil prices and JPY weakness to gradually emerge as upside pressure. But it is important to remember that the Fed did this to control inflation, which also disproportionately impacts lower-income households. …But will likely not correct it directly Chair Warsh has alluded to wanting to close this divergence via monetary policy. His preferred way of dealing with this is via a smaller balance sheet. However, evidence is mixed on that front. Also, in our view, the Fed is unlikely to view the existence of a K- shaped economy as, on its own, a reason to drive monetary policy decision making. Risk of policy miscalibration in a K-shaped economy Reflation or stagflation? A policy calibration challenge Additionally, we don’t think Fed policy can fix this problem either. A K-shaped economy increases the risk that policymakers misread aggregate signals because different income groups are experiencing very different macro environments. For higher-income households, strong balance sheets, asset gains and relatively resilient spending resemble a reflationary environment, supporting demand and keeping parts of the services sector firm. For lower-income households, however, the combination of supply-side shocks, elevated borrowing costs and limited financial buffers feels closer to mild stagflation: growth is weaker, labor market conditions are softer, and purchasing power remains under pressure even if softer demand ultimately leads to somewhat lower inflation. This divergence creates a policy dilemma.

records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 3 Introduction This edition of our Global Exposure Guide provides an update on foreign revenue and cost exposure by region. The guide serves as a reference for investors, particularly in times of regional instability that can arise on short notice. It is based on a proprietary database built using estimates generated by Morgan Stanley's fundamental analysts and is not available anywhere else. Our Global Exposure Guide database includes foreign revenue exposure on both an aggregate and stock-level basis. The aggregate view allows us to look at revenue exposure from a macro perspective and see which areas of the economy are most exposed when global events impact multinational companies. However, it is very important to look at stock-level data because the aggregates are influenced by large cap companies (the exposure estimates are weighted by consensus 2026 sales estimates). For these companies, exposure to any one region experiencing instability can have a very large impact on sales. AUD positioning is no longer long, extending room for AUD to resume outperformance. On the demand side, AI-related workloads, particularly within hyperscale data centers, are driving outsized requirements for both high-performance DRAM and NAND storage, with long-context model training and inference creating incremental storage intensity per unit of compute. At the same time, supply remains effectively constrained: manufacturers have been slow to bring incremental wafer capacity back online and continue to prioritize higher-margin products (such as HBM and server-grade DRAM), which has limited availability of more commoditized memory categories. The net result is a tighter supply-demand balance across the broader memory complex, supporting broad-based price increases. Looking ahead, pricing likely remains supported near term, though the pace of increases may begin to moderate as the cycle progresses. While AI-driven demand appears durable, the industry is inherently cyclical, and producers are already signaling gradual capacity normalization over the next several years via both utilization increases and targeted capex. First, we decompose the Treasury yield curve into its first two principal components (capturing the dominant level and slope dynamics), and then we explain each component with macro-financial drivers via OLS regressions. Although the BEA's upcoming annual update in September will likely revise inflation lower for the computer software and accessories category, and quality-adjustment concerns may warrant some look-through, we think the Fed is unlikely to ignore the impulse entirely, especially if other slices of core PCE inflation remain elevated. • AI inflation is more a PCE problem than a CPI-markets issue, due largely to its negligible weight in the CPI. However, there could be second-order effects based on how the Fed interprets the PCE price data. records.text: 2 US Economic Viewpoint | 29 June 2026 Executive Summary In a previous report (K, but why? Five drivers of K-shaped spending), we showed how consumer spending since late-’24/early-’25 became increasingly K-shaped, with higher- income households driving activity amid widening divergence across income cohorts (Exhibit 1). We documented five factors responsible for the K-shaped spending dynamics – balance sheets, housing costs, the labor market, fiscal stimulus and the affordability shock from higher gas prices. Together, these left higher-income households supported by equity wealth, stable housing costs and steadier labor outcomes, while lower-income households faced rising rents, weaker job growth and higher debt burdens. Then in 2026, this divergence widened further: higher-income spending received a larger boost from OBBBA-related tax relief, while higher energy prices from the Iran shock, acting as a regressive tax weighed more heavily on lower-income households, leaving the former better positioned to absorb the hit. In this report, we turn to the implications of this divergence. We first assess why K- shaped dynamics matter for aggregate consumption outcomes, highlighting the outsized share of higher-income households in overall spending. We then show how these K- shaped dynamics help reconcile the disconnect between a cooling labor market and resilient consumer spending we got last year. Also, we use the pandemic recovery to learn about the current K-shaped cycle. Final

The labor market slowdown has lowered income growth. Real spending growth continues to handily outpace income, as wealth supports financing spending from saving. • The US consumer continues to spend. Spending has slowed on net from the robust pace of 2024, but not nearly as much as real disposable income growth. • Households across all income groups expect to be more sensitive to future inflation now than in 2022. records.text: European Equity Strategy29 June 2026 ab 12 Switzerland's Economic Outlook 2026-27 Inflation: Modest pickup, but only due to energy Inflation remained unchanged at 0.6% y/y in May and is still largely driven by energy. This is likely the peak of the energy-driven increase for now, with inflation expected to hover around 0.5% throughout the summer before picking up moderately to around 1% in Q4. Inflation pressures are expected to remain contained because of offsetting forces from a still strong CHF, Switzerland’s lower energy weight in the CPI and limited risks of second-round inflation via wages amid a weakened labour market. Overall, we expect inflation to average 0.5% in 2026 and 0.7% in 2027/28. Growth: Through the trough, but return to trend growth only next year After just 0.2% q/q growth in Q4 and a contraction in Q3 '25, the Swiss economy expanded strongly in Q1 '26, growing 0.7% q/q. This was partly boosted by licensing income from the Winter Olympics but also by solid manufacturing activity, which benefitted from catch-up effects after last year’s high US tariffs. Meanwhile, private consumption stagnated in Q1. Going forward, we are sceptical how long the modest manufacturing recovery can last in light of the energy shock and expect industrial momentum to weaken from here, so that overall growth will likely run somewhat below trend in coming quarters. Key Takeaways The USD/JPY rally has shifted from yen weakness to broad USD strength. This distinction matters for intervention risk, as authorities are typically more sensitive to speculative yen selling than to generalized USD appreciation. Intervention risk has increased, but imminent action does not yet appear likely. The MoF has stepped up verbal warnings, but has not yet characterized recent FX moves as clearly “speculative.” USD/JPY looks close to fair value on our three-factor framework. The key inputs remain US terminal-rate pricing, global risk sentiment, and Japan’s terms of trade. Lower oil prices and weak global risk sentiment are supportive for the yen outside USD crosses. We remain neutral on JPY given the concern for the potential intervention and await a clearer dip-buying opportunity. Risks (and opportunity): narrow breadth, retail speculation, over-optimism, primary market supply Our core view on regional equities remains constructive, driven by a supportive macro backdrop, rapid earnings growth, and mid-cycle valuations. However, there are several risks that warrant close monitoring. First, market leadership has been very narrow. 8 stocks account for 96% of the MXAPJ index’s ytd gains, with heavyweight semiconductors stocks contributing a majority of the region’s performance. Changes in the outlook for this cohort will have an outsized impact on the aggregate index. Second, retail speculation has increased, notably in Korea where index and single stock leveraged ETF assets under management have risen from $5bn at the start of the year to over $40bn at present. We had expected the MPC to be proactive to counter the possibility of second round effects, given above- target inflation in past few years, high inflation expectations and UK’s past susceptibility to inflation persistence. But it appears to us that the BoE would only act if the energy shock is prolonged or clear, strong evidence emerges on signs of second round effects, risks of which it judges is higher the longer high energy prices persist. The BoE looks to be taking comfort from tightening in financial conditions and the Bank Rate being restrictive. This suggests the MPC is willing to tolerate above target inflation temporarily, as long as second round effects are contained. Even with some second-round effects, the MPC has kept the option of holding rates for longer open (instead of hiking) in this paragraph in the June MPC minutes- “However, there would be a more challenging trade- off if higher energy prices appeared to be feeding into more persistent domestic inflation. In that event, the weight placed on output stabilisation would be likely to diminish, and policy would need to remain restrictive for longer, or become more restrictive.” This implies a higher bar for hikes. The MXAPJ index gained 21%, the 4th best 1H and 3rd best 2Q in its 39-year history. However, the gains were driven by the tech hardware-heavy north Asian markets of Korea (+119%) and Taiwan (+56%). Ex-these markets, the rest of the region declined 9%, with Indonesia (-40%), offshore China (-18%) and India (-10%) falling most. Japan also posted a strong 1H but with similar technology leadership. Topix gained a commendable 16%, but the more tech-focused Nikkei index rose 38%, its third best 1H and best quarterly performance (in 2Q) ever. This backdrop prompts queries on whether tech-led momentum will persist in the second half of 2026 or if there will be a rotation in leadership to other markets or sectors. Our view is that north Asian markets will continue to lead given the strength of their underlying thematic drivers and the strong earnings they are delivering. These center on tech hardware but also include adjacent areas such as power and defense. We summarize our views and highlight risks investors should monitor in the points that follow. records.text: 4 US Economic Viewpoint | 29 June 2026 concentration means that aggregate consumption outcomes are increasingly dictated by higher-income financial health, balance sheet dynamics and cost pressures. Aggregate demand becomes less sensitive to lower-income stress This asymmetry helps explain why aggregate consumption can remain resilient even as lower-income households face pressures from higher rents, elevated debt-servicing costs, weaker labor market outcomes, and greater exposure to energy price shocks. As long as higher-income consumers who are more insulated from these pressures and more exposed to equity wealth, tax relief, and higher-income continue to spend, headline consumption growth can mask underlying stress elsewhere in the economy. A BEA-BLS study reinforces this point. Today, when many of the post-pandemic dynamics and policy shocks operate asymmetrically, the rising concentration of spending at the top makes aggregate consumption less sensitive to conditions facing lower-income households. As a result, traditional signals of consumer weakening, such as rising delinquencies or softer hiring among lower-wage workers may coexist with steady overall spending, complicating real time assessments of consumer health from the perspective of the broader economy. records.text: 26 June 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 25 Do quarter-end pension flows flatten the curve? Steven Zeng, CFA | Strategist | +1-212-250-9373 Conventional market view suggests that pension and index -related fixed income buying around quarter -end tends to flatten the Treasury curve. We examine the historical evidence. We test this hypothesis using a combination of regression and event analysis. To control for factors that could influence the 10s -30s curve, we first regress the one-day change in 10s -30s on changes in Fed expectations (proxied by the 2y yield), risk sentiment (S&P 500 returns), and oil price changes. These 3 factors are all highly significant, and residuals from the regression thus represent changes in the 10s-30s curve not explained by these macro drivers, for example rebalancing flows. We then analyze these residuals over a 5-day event window surrounding quarter- ends (t -3 to t+1) since 2000. On average, the 10s -30s residual flattened by approximately 0.5bp between t -1 and t0, with the timing consistent with actual observed quarter -end buying. To further assess the impact of rebalancing, we sort quarter -end observations by the size of pension flows (sourced from the Fed’s quarterly flow of funds data), which we then divide by the amount of 20y+ Treasuries outstanding to control for market growth. records.text: US Outlook More mirage than momentum Incoming data continue to fuel a reacceleration narrative, but we interpret much of this as a mirage. Though GDP and PCE headlines look firm, underlying demand and income fundamentals look softer. We maintain our call that the Fed remains on indefinite hold, with risks clearly skewed toward hikes. • Activity data exaggerate the extent of re-acceleration, with upward revisions to headline Q1• GDP growth driven by the volatile trade component masking evidence that underlying momentum has softened. Private domestic final purchases were marked down to 1.7% q/q saar and consumer spending to 0.5%, reinforcing a gradual downtrend in domestic demand. • The rebound of PCE in Q2 looks fragile and exaggerated by special factors, including• carryover effects, event-driven boosts, and the lack of timely source data for service categories. Underlying income developments remain subdued despite the pickup in measured job gains. As these influences fade, we expect spending growth to settle at ~1.5% q/q saar in H2 2026. • Inflation still seems poised to soften in the coming months, but upside risks remain. After• firming to 0.32% m/m in May, core PCE should round down toward 0.20% m/m in June as financial services effects unwind. Against this backdrop, Fed communications are placing greater weight on inflation risks, leaving policy on hold for the foreseeable future, with risks tilted toward hikes. records.text: US Leveraged Loans Mid-year supply update: Less opportunistic supply ahead We cut our 2026 leveraged loan supply outlook to $435bn ($480-520bn previously) based on a weaker 1H and a tougher rates backdrop ahead. While refinancing remains supportive given a heavy maturity wall, reduced opportunistic activity and softer M&A temper overall issuance expectations. We are lowering our FY26 loan supply forecast to $425-445bn from $480-520bn, reflecting a softer 1H and expectations for a less accommodating rates backdrop in 2H. While year-to-date issuance remains broadly in line with recent years, weaker forward conditions constrain the full- year outlook. Refinancing activity remains the dominant driver but is revised lower, now expected to be $190-210bn, versus $220-240bn prior. A large and front-loaded maturity wall should still push refinancing higher into 2H, but fewer opportunistic channels (eg, loan-for-bond or private credit takeouts) and a higher-for-longer rates path limit upside. M&A-related issuance is tracking higher as a share of supply but is unlikely to sustain its 1H pace, with FY26 now projected at $80-100bn. A less supportive rates backdrop and a thinner forward deal pipeline point to a moderation in activity in 2H. LBO supply remains steady at $70-90bn, but momentum is expected to slow into year-end. The surge in AI-related imports - already elevated in volume terms -is likely to strengthen further in dollar terms because of chip-linked price effects. This fact underscores the need to put the current capex cycle into a context of imports, especially for computing and electronics. The surge in imports is not uniform. Imports across a broader set of capital goods have declined some, even with US manufacturing firming. The divergence between US activity and imports will stay a theme. There is very little evidence of reshoring on a large scale. The capex the US is doing is not generally from US produced output. If reshoring were to pick up, therefore, we would expect imports to have to rise first, in order to create the capacity to produce the capital goods onshore. As we recently argued , the repricing in Fed expectations has brought front -end USD rates broadly in line with our t op-down assessment of neutral . At the same time, US data surprise indicators and equity markets have moved off their highs. On the inflation side, market pricing is relatively benign: 2y USD CPI is currently just above 2.30%, pointing to US inflation expectations broadly at target over the next two years, while forwards such as 2y1y are at the low end of their 1y range. Meanwhile, macro factors continue to support higher term premia, particularly in real rates (see here). Against this backdrop, we see scope for a steeper USD 2s10s real yield curve, which inverted this week (Figure left). A rise in inflation pricing would tend to benefit this spread (Figure right), as would a steepening in the nominal curve. The key risk to the trade is a further decline in oil prices, which would mechanically steepen the USD CPI curve while having a more limited impact on the nominal curve. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 11 Revenue Exposure to Europe Of foreign sources of revenue, companies in our database have the highest exposure to Europe at 11% ( Exhibit 12 ). At the sector level, Tech has the highest exposure to Europe at 21% ( Exhibit 13 ) and is closely followed by Materials at 20%. One thing to note is that this exposure represents an important source of end demand for Tech companies. These companies are not manufacturing intermediate goods in Europe for use as inputs in products sold elsewhere; they are generating revenue from final goods sold in the region. Software & Services is driving this exposure, and Software companies are deriving 23% of their revenue from Europe. Consumer Discretionary, Communication Services, and Industrials all have revenue exposure to Europe in the double digits. Consumer Staples is not among the most exposed sectors but two of its industry groups generate a substantial percent of revenue in Europe. The Household & Personal Products industry group generates 20% of revenue there while that figure is 21% for Food, Beverage & Tobacco. The break below 1.14 suggests clearer technical momentum to the downside and given the widespread investor skepticism about the European outlook, we think EUR will be used as a key funder for both USD longs and cyclical currency longs. That said, we think FX vol markets are underestimating the potential volatility in the pair, particularly to the topside as we think investors underestimate that the Fed's reaction function is more symmetric than they think. EUR is particularly attractive as a long in a state of the world where USD-negative risk premium is increasing again, and we will be watching the US policymaking process closely, particularly as it relates to the composition of the FOMC, as this could be a key catalyst for a return to investors pricing in greater risk premium in the USD and favoring other peer reserve currencies like the EUR. records.text: Nikolaj.Lippmann@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-2463 We publish the 11th edition of the global version of one of our most popular and requested products, the Global Exposure Guide. This report quantifies the geographic revenue exposure of companies across the US, Europe, Japan and EM, using Morgan Stanley analyst estimates to provide a consistent global framework where company disclosure is often limited. Our Global Exposure Guide collection explores one of Morgan Stanley's 4 Key Themes for 2026 – Investing for a Multipolar World. In its 29th edition, our data on geographic exposures across >3,300 stocks globally can be more helpful to investors than ever amid today's geopolitical and supply chain shifts. The most notable shift this year is the sharp rise in EM ex-China foreign revenue exposure, which has increased from c.44% last year to c.51% in 2026, led particularly by South Korea and Taiwan’s rising exposure to the US in the semiconductor sector. To help investors capture this theme, we include a new South Korea exposure screen. For North America, we find that companies in our database derive 27% of revenue from foreign sources, with the largest source being Europe at 12%, followed by Asia ex-Japan & ex-China at 5%, Latin America at 4%, and China at 3%. The sectors with the highest foreign revenue exposure are Tech (54%), Materials (47%), Comm. Services (30%), and Industrials (29%). records.text: US Investment Grade Boosting our supply forecast We revise our FY26 US IG supply forecast to $1.9trn, with net issuance just short of $1trn. Both would be record levels. The upgrade reflects the very large funding needs for the AI ecosystem. This matters for valuations, as issuance continues to be a key driver of returns. For our latest US high grade company rating changes, click here. For our sector ratings, click here. We raise our FY26 supply forecast to $1.9trn, from $1.6trn, 32% above 2025 and above the prior $1.66trn record in 2020. Net issuance should reach about $970bn, up close to 2x y/y and equaling the 2020 record (see Figure 2). Supply is running red hot versus last year after netting maturities and coupons. Year-to- date gross issuance is up roughly one-third versus 2025 and close to 2020 levels. Net issuance is almost double last year’s pace, while issuance net of maturities and coupons is at the highest level outside of 2020 and roughly four times 2025 (Figure 4). The marginal dollar of supply is increasingly tied to the AI ecosystem. Tech and AI-related issuers have driven much of the y/y increase, especially in longer maturities. They represent 18% of the year-to-date IG issuance and 37% when focusing on 10y+ only. Several AI-linked sectors have already issued more than their full-year FY26 maturities. We treat historical implied volatility time series – including ATM volatility, risk reversal/skew and butterfly – as tradeable assets . Given the outsized contribution this category has made to core PCE in recent months, even a partial correction could take some air out of recent measures of PCE price inflation, particularly in early 2026. Our early analysis suggest that these changes, taken together, would modestly lower the path of core PCE inflation, though the magnitudes are uncertain. In principle, changes could potentially eliminate a fair bit—but not nearly all—of the recent inflationary run-up, with these categories having contributed roughly 0.4pp to the 4q% rate of core PCE price inflation in Q1 ( Figure 6). More plausibly, we think the changes would likely subtract a few tenths from measured %y/y inflation over the five-year revision window, and perhaps halve the 5-6bp contribution of the computer software and accessories category to %m/m core PCE price inflation from December 2025 through April 2026. Although this might downplay the need for Fed hikes on the margin, we still expect a range of measures to show that underlying inflation is running notably faster than the 2% target, implying that the revisions are best viewed more as a refinement than an engineered decline. Should payroll gains outperform our expectations and push the unemployment rate below the median FOMC participants' estimate of the longer run neutral rate (4.2%), then the Fed may decide a more restrictive stance is needed to prevent labor market overheating. We think a move below 4.0% on the unemployment rate by September would increase cause for concern that the labor market is much stronger than thought. Finally, we also acknowledge that data may not be the deciding factor for some participants. A year ago, the Fed viewed its policy stance as inappropriate in light of their view that downside risk to employment outweighed upside risk to inflation. Some of the nine projections for rate hikes may reflect a reversal in this risk management approach; they may see the distribution of risks as skewed sufficiently in the direction of firmer inflation and view the current policy stance as inappropriate. In other words, subjective assessments about the distribution of outcomes around the modal path may be enough for hikes, diminishing the influence of incoming data. For now, we retain our outlook for no rate hikes from the Fed this year. While incoming data since the June FOMC have made us marginally more comfortable in this view, we remain attentive to the data and will adjust our views accordingly as the economy evolves. records.text: ould take some air out of AI-inflation Late last week, the BEA posted a preview of the upcoming 2026 annual revisions to the National Economic Accounts (NEA) on its website. Among the several updates planned, three salient source-data updates are in train for the PCE price index, namely to: 1) legal services ; 2) portfolio management and investment advisory services and 3) computer software and accessories. The updates will be applied to the revision window Q1 21 to Q1 26, on September 30. For the purposes of this note, we focus on the "computer software and accessories" category. The BEA intends to replace the current CPI deflator with a composite deflator that includes the existing CPI deflator, along with PPI for gaming software; and PPI for hosting, ASP and other IT infrastructure. The motivation is to address the alleged misalignment in subcomponents for the CPI and PCE categories, which has also been highlighted in the Fed staff paper referenced above. Indeed, the BEA's latest available PCE bridge table suggests that the PCE computer software and accessories category does not include blank media such as flash drives, which the CPI category includes, and is likely the driver of recent inflation. It is unclear what weights the BEA will assign to these new deflators, given there is little-to-no public information about the weights for "software" versus "accessories" in this category. Therefore, we produce a simple, equal-weight proxy and compare against the current series.

records.text: M Idea 2 The Data Road Map to Rate Hikes We expect a Fed-on-hold through year-end Following the June FOMC meeting, we retained our outlook for a Fed on hold in 2026 despite 9 FOMC participants who submitted a projection with at least one rate hike this year. We retained our baseline outlook for no rate hikes for several reasons. First, our forecast for inflation is more sanguine. We believe tariff pass through is ending, paving the way for substantial disinflation in core goods over the next year, and the recently signed MOU between the US and Iran has helped push oil prices back toward pre-conflict levels. In addition, we look for further moderation in shelter inflation and some payback from residual seasonality into year end. On net, and following the release of May PCE inflation, our forecast of 4Q/4Q headline and core PCE inflation of 3.2% and 3.0% this year is substantially below the median FOMC participant. Second, we suspect that FOMC participants' projections may be overstating inflation pressures. In March, FOMC participants had to form their inflation projections shortly after the conflict began. Without knowing the duration of the conflict, participants likely underestimated how much inflation would firm in subsequent months. In June, we think the Fed may be overstating inflation pressures since forecasts were likely formed before the MOU took hold. We revise this component of our supply forecast down modestly, to a midpoint of $200bn, which still represents an acceleration of refinancing activity in 2H26. One major factor in this is the front-loaded nature of the BSL market's maturity wall. As shown in Figure 6, the proportions of the LLI with less than two and less than three years to maturity are both the highest in over 10 years, at 8% and 23%, respectively. The core of our approach to estimating refinancing supply is relatively mechanical. We first analyze the historical rate at which each tower of the BSL market's maturity wall gets paid down each year. For example, we look at the 1-2y tower and find that over the subsequent 12 months, it has been reduced in size by 73% each year since 2007. The domestic demand stock universe is heavily skewed toward certain industries, such as retail, land transportation, real estate, and electric power & gas, so some of the factor returns indicated in Exhibit 28 may reflect industry effects. We therefore also show the results after neutralizing by GICS industry group, in Exhibit 29 . The main conclusions are the same as those in Exhibit 28 ; the B/P factor continued show consistently strong performance even after industry neutralization, suggesting that the value effect for domestic demand stocks is likely to reflect valuation differences within industries and not just industry bias. At the same time, even after industry neutralization, it is difficult to confirm sustained effectiveness for factors such as share price momentum and EPS revisions. In light of this, we think our findings confirm that an effective approach to stock selection within domestic demand stocks has been one focused not only on industry allocation but also identifying particular stocks that have been left undervalued within the relevant industries.

Derivative hedges to navigate correction risk The strong 1H performance of Korea and Taiwan raises the risk of a sharp pullback, particularly given high market concentration, increases in retail speculative positioning, and greater optimism regarding the AI tech hardware theme. We remain strategically positive on both markets as noted above but recognize they are extended and vulnerable to profit taking, as our refreshed Regional Asia Drawdown Risk model (RADaR) indicates. We therefore view derivative overlays as attractive ways to cushion downside risk and shape positively skewed outcomes. We favor put spread collars on KOSPI200 and TWSE indices at zero cost. The combination of increased volatility and a reduction in put/call skew results in attractive structures to hedge downside risk without giving up too much upside. For example, selling a 132% Dec call on KOSPI2 can fund a 90%/70% put spread, with broadly comparable pricing for TWSE. Given the 6m duration of this structure, theta decay will not build until later in the year, whereas a pullback in markets would likely result in rising vega and gamma, suggesting investors would be protected at least partially even if the index does not fall 10% to the 90% put strike level. Alternatively, a simple 95%/85% Dec put spread on the Nikkei index is indicatively priced at 3.35%, which would also provide protection against a pullback in Korea and Taiwan given the 70% correlation with these indices. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 26 June 2026 Citi Research 6 There has been no discussion of where the Japanese economy is positioned. The “current projection case” assumes that only the effect of demand growth due to additional fiscal expenditure of ¥10trn is realized, in which case the inflation rate would trend toward 2%. The BoJ statement, however, says that trend consumer price inflation is expected to steadily accelerate to a level largely consistent with the price stability target in FY3/27 H2 through FY3/28, and then remain at that level. This does not include things for which the legal structure is not in place. Under the economic and fiscal model used in government estimates, if real government expenditure is increased by 1% of real GDP and if the level relative to GDP is maintained, consumer price in five years’ time would increase by 0.76%. This would be around 0.15% annually, or some 0.23% of the ¥10trn expenditure. Including growth investment would further boost the inflation outlook. The estimate is that both short-term and long-term interest rates would be boosted by more than 0.5ppt in five years’ time. In other words, both the neutral interest rate and long-term interest rates would increase. An increase in TFP would work in the opposite direction. That is, if the government acts as scheduled, both the inflation outlook and the interest rate outlook are likely to rise. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 26 June 2026 Citi Research 3 The government has announced its roadmap for the investment of ¥370trn in 17 strategic areas. While some more details have been disclosed since last week, the bulk remains unknown. The division in investment between the public and private sectors in particular is unclear, so it is impossible to foresee how much JGB issuance would be required from next fiscal year onward. Estimates of the impact on fiscal positions assume ¥10trn annually for the real increase in fiscal expenditure. This includes the investment in crisis management and growth strategies for which a funding source has not yet been secured as well as spending previously included in supplementary budgets. We think most of this can be covered without JGB issuance via bullish estimates of tax revenue and a clear reduction in the balance of front-loaded bonds. However, bridging JGBs are not included. We think a reasonable estimate would be for an increase in JGB issuance of more than ¥10trn, and the biggest increase is likely in the initial fiscal year. In defense the roadmap mainly reflects investment in dual-use technology. For small drones and naval vessels the roadmap states that future investment is expected in a revision to the three basic documents governing Japan’s security and foreign relations. records.text: two cuts in Mar/Jun-27 and ultimately more to 1.50% terminal depo in 2028. The macro narrative is unchanged. Structural challenges and chronic demand insufficiency, paired with ECB policy that is likely too tight, suggest a persistent inflation undershoot, eventually pushing the central bank into cuts below 2%. Growth: less bad, but still not exactly good Lower oil and gas prices reduce the damage from the energy crisis. The growth recovery is likely to start earlier, and permanent GDP loss is likely to be smaller than previously assumed. Our GDP growth forecast moves to 0.5% this year (-20bp) and 1.3% in 2027 (+10bp). We extend our horizon to 2028, now expecting 1.1%. The cut to this year’s growth expectation is due to the -0.2% qoq contraction in 1Q26 driven by Ireland. Big swings in Irish GDP have become frequent, but erratic. We stay agnostic about “if and when” the 1Q26 contribution of Ireland to the Euro area reverses. That may create some mechanical upside risks to forecasts this year. We have raised sequential growth from here due to better consumption and capex prospects (Exhibit 2). Let’s be clear: the shock of the energy crisis has now possibly halved compared to our initial expectations in early April (when we assumed oil prices would remain close to USD 100 per barrel and natural gas at EUR 80 or more for most of this year). But we are still facing a c 40bp cumulative GDP growth loss over 2026-27 vs pre-Iran war expectations (excluding the Irish effect on 1Q26).

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Oil Tracker: US ending stocks of crude oil edge lower amid increased exports and unchanged production We continue to track the evolution of petroleum-product inventory and production. US stocks of crude oil and petroleum products, which represent the EIA's estimate of how many barrels of oil and petroleum products are physically sitting in US storage at period end, continue to move lower. Inclusive of the SPR, inventory is falling by about 2mn barrels a day. The spot price of oil for immediate purchase and delivery in the physical market remains high despite futures prices declining since the MOU between the US and Iran. US domestic crude production has edged modestly higher in recent weeks, but it remains about in line with pre-conflict production. Net imports of oil (imports - exports) are declining because of increased oil exports. records.text: US Economic Viewpoint | 29 June 2026 9 Why the data send mixed signals in a K-shaped economy A K-shaped economy effectively combines a demand boom for higher-income households with stagflation like conditions for everyone else. An important implication is that macro indicators that weigh individuals equally, such as payrolls, the unemployment rate, aggregate wage growth or consumer sentiment had been signaling a more downside risk than indicators that weigh households by their spending power, such as GDP, aggregate consumption or inflation. In an environment where higher-income households account for a disproportionate share of total spending and are also the most insulated from labor market and price shocks, measures tied to demand and output can remain firm even as labor market breadth deteriorates. We think this helps explain some of the data conundrums observed since last year, including robust GDP growth supported by solid spending alongside softer payroll growth, rising entry-level unemployment and weaker sentiment. The good news is that a lot of these labor market indicators look like they are now on the path towards recovery. Monetary policy implications from a K- shaped economy Short-term policy response Did the Fed cause the K? If yes, should it correct it? Since March 2022, as inflation surged, the Fed has raised rates by a net 350bp. Even after cuts in 2024 and 2025, policy rates remain elevated at 3.50-3.75%, well above pre- pandemic lows. records.text: administered by the IRS and state housing agencies, it is the largest source of affordable housing finance in the US, supporting over 90% of new affordable rental units. There are two types of LIHTC credits. The 9% credit is designed to cover a large portion of a project’s equity needs, significantly reducing required leverage, and these projects are not required to use tax-exempt bonds, and to a large degree rely on bank loans. The 4% credit is available when a project finances at least 50% of total costs with tax-exempt private activity bonds, which was decreased to 25% by the OBBBA. In a typical 4% LIHTC transaction, tax-exempt bonds fund just over half of project costs (generally 50–55%), triggering tax credits that are sold to investors—primarily banks and insurance companies—and converted into equity (in some of the new transactions this number might decline). This structure benefits from a meaningful equity cushion (~35–40%), oversight from equity investors, and stable, restricted rent flows, contributing to historically low default rates. Some transactions are further enhanced by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac credit support or FHA/GNMA insurance; however, this support is generally provided at the mortgage level rather than the bond level. At the other end of the spectrum are single-asset project financings and workforce housing bonds, which rely more directly on property-level cash flows and carry higher credit risk. records.text: FX Strategy: JPY-selling catalyst shifts from war to Warsh Shinichiro Kadota BSJL, Japan | Lhamsuren Sharavdemberel BSJL, Japan This week has seen USDJPY trade in the upper-161s amid elevated vigilance around the prospect of FX intervention. Although oil prices have fallen back to pre-Iran war levels, the catalyst for JPY selling has shifted from higher oil prices to a hawkish Fed, and the JPY is testing its 2024 lows. MoF officials have repeatedly warned against JPY weakness, and BoJ officials have continued to send hawkish messages, but their efforts have failed to support JPY. We updated our quarterly outlook this week, raising our USDJPY forecast to the lower-160s. FX supply-demand dynamics remain structurally tilted to net selling, with JPY20trn in net yen selling annually (as a result of a JPY20trn CA surplus and JPY40trn in outward investment). Household portfolio reallocation to overseas investment assets amid higher inflation is proving persistent, as foreign-asset investment trusts under the new NISA tax exemption scheme are about JPY10trn annually, with further upside risks from children’s NISA in 2027. Additionally, our FDI model suggests outbound direct investment will remain high in 2026, with only a partial offset from inward FDI flows. While MoF FX intervention between late April and May, totaling JPY11.7trn, absorbed about a half of this imbalance, another round of intervention would be needed fully to offset this underlying JPY selling pressure. Currently, this index accounts for just under 2% of core PCE. The current methodology for this component involves deflating nominal expenditures on portfolio management services with the PPI index for portfolio management fees. We explained last week how this tends to reflect changes in asset prices (mostly equities) from the start of one month to the next. The new methodology will involve estimating the quantity of these services consumed (real expenditures) using payroll employment for the portfolio management and investment advice industry. Presumably, nominal portfolio management expenditures and the new estimate for real expenditures would then be used to back-out portfolio management prices. In our rough estimations, we calculate these new prices as the difference between current nominal expenditures on portfolio management services and aggregate hours worked in the portfolio management and investment advice industry. Nominal expenditures of portfolio management services are a very important part of this calculation and it is unclear to us if the new methodology involves meaningful changes to nominal expenditures. Typically, those committees approve decisions by the working groups that sit a level below them in the structure. • July 8, 2026: The NAIC's Financial Condition (E) Committee will vote whether to approve the proposal. The more complex question, however, is around leakages: how much of the boost is genuinely additional rather than merely redistributed – either as a substitute or temporally? Spend that's shifted toward hospitality during a sporting event may be diverted from other categories (leaving overall spending net neutral). Moreover, any jump in activity observed during the World Cup may come from households pulling forward spending into the tournament window, and therefore repaid by softness immediately afterwards. A second drag may come from productivity and hours worked: matches played in distant time zones can depress productivity in the day or days after. Equally, games abroad could see a meaningful outflow of residents, diverting spend away from the local/domestic economy as the tournament progresses. What's our approach to estimating the World Cup boost? We set out two quantitative approaches to estimate the effect of a potential World Cup GDP boost. Both approaches are conditioned on past football tournaments (Euros and World Cup) going back to 2000. records.text: o some extent. US households as compared to Europeans ones benefited from unprecedented fiscal transfers that boosted household savings, often referred to as “excess savings”. While excess savings have now largely been depleted, they peaked at close to $2.2tr (Exhibit 10). This fiscal support helps explain some of the strength of the post-pandemic US consumer and, by extension, the outperformance of US economic growth relative to the more “sluggish recovery” in Europe where support was less “cash in hand ”. Role of foreign demand and corporate savings However, the mechanism extends beyond household balance sheets alone. Large fiscal deficits were supported in part by continued foreign demand for US assets, while strong corporate profitability also helped sustain investment and employment. Against this backdrop, differences in household balance-sheet strength, wealth accumulation and spending capacity widened across income groups, contributing to the emergence of today's K-shaped economy. Lessons for today The history lesson is particularly relevant because it in part shaped the current environment. Large macro shocks kept interacting with an unequal distribution of financial buffers and asset gains that, despite more retail participation in equities, benefited higher-income groups. Meanwhile, strong corporate balance sheets helped sustain investment and labor demand. Combined, this eventually led to the K-shaped consumer of today. -50 0 50 100 150 200 250 Jan-'23 Apr-'23 Jul-

We note that the HSCEI tends to strongly correlate with the China 5y (see Figure 3). In the 1 June QTOW, we introduced a China 5y payer trade idea. This suggests to us that a move higher in China 5y could translate to a rebound in the HSCEI. We therefore like to be tactically long HSCEI, targeting its MarFA™ Macro fair value of 8277.7. The model uses the share of index par maturing in the next three years, the gap between index yield-to-worst and index coupon, and the share of bonds trading to call. records.text: Q2 2026 earnings season preview The importance of earnings strength in lifting US equities this year puts the onus on the upcoming Q2 2026 reporting season to help extend the market rally. Earnings have arithmetically accounted for the entire S&P 500 gain this year. In fact, during the last 12 months, the S&P 500 has rallied by 18% with no increase in the forward P/E multiple, which now stands at 20x. We expect Q2 reports will reveal another quarter of strong earnings growth, supported by a solid macro backdrop and the ongoing AI investment boom. Q2 nominal GDP growth is tracking at 7% year/year, and Micron’s earnings report this week was a reminder of the continued earnings strength across the AI infrastructure complex. Earnings revision breadth during the past month has remained solidly positive, with upward revisions outnumbering downward revisions in every sector except for Consumer Discretionary. Financials will kick off the Q2 2026 earnings season the week of July 13th. By the first week of August, roughly 75% of S&P 500 market cap will have reported results. Nvidia (NVDA), the largest stock in the market, will report on August 26th. We look for a similar contribution in the June data. To us, this suggests not only more underlying strength, but also a more limited payback effect to come in the jobs statistics later this summer. ▪ Sturdy earnings growth: We look for a 0.3% m/m rise in average hourly earnings (3.5% y/y versus 3.4% y/y prior). We see the Fed as unconcerned about wage-price dynamics presently, particularly with productivity running at a solid clip, but that might enter the conversation if unemployment pushes below 4%. The Fed’s latest Beige Book suggest ed that inflation itself is driving worker demands for higher wages, as “Districts reported more frequent wage adjustments and cost-of-living increases to manage increasing fuel and other household cost pressures”. ▪ Unemployment rate may tick down to 4.2%: We look for a drop in the unemployment rate to 4.2%, the lowest in a year. We still see our 0-20k breakeven pace as valid, despite the apparent gap between strong payrolls year to date (114k on average) and only a 0.1pp drop in the unemployment rate over that span. The household survey has posted an average YTD pace of employment growth of about 42k, which is consistent with the observed drop in the jobless rate. The net upshot has been a rally in duration this week as breakevens have developed greater downward momentum amid an apparent easing of inflation concerns. Stick with core themes Our strongest view throughout the uncertainty and capricious newsflow of the Iran war has been to focus on structural themes that are unlikely to be affected by near-term events. Following strong performance of many of these themes, there is a temptation to rotate towards areas that have underperformed. We favor remaining aligned with core themes, recognizing that there may be some temporary corrective phases. In brief, our favored themes are: AI beneficiaries: Infrastructure supply chain. The semiconductor memory n supercycle is one of the most powerful and prominent themes that is still not fully priced. Accelerating agentic AI-driven demand for compute, which our semiconductor analysts estimate at 24x growth in global token demand by 2030, is outstripping memory supply: this year’s record DRAM and NAND supply shortfall is likely to increase further in 2027 and remain deeply negative in 2028 and possibly into 2029-30. This is driving sharp increases in memory prices which flow to outsized bottom line gains for memory producers given the industry’s high operating leverage. In turn, this shortage is rippling through the hardware supply chain. Our AIGC Hardware (GSSZAIHW) and Semiconductor (GSSZAISM) baskets offer broad exposure to this dynamic. Possible links to defense spending increases The latest strategic investment could also be related to future discussions on increasing defense spending. Japan currently has a target for defense spending of 2% of FY2022 GDP , but the US is calling on its allies to raise spending to 3.5% of GDP , on a par with NATO, in terms of core defense spending excluding related costs ( Figure 5). As a result, it appears highly likely that the target for the defense spending/GDP ratio will be raised in revisions to the three national security documents scheduled this year. On 24 June, the LDP and the Japan Innovation Party each handed PM Takaichi recommendations for the revision of the three security documents. Discussions within the government will now move into full swing. Because increasing defense spending would have a large fiscal impact (in our analysis, if the new target is 3.5% of GDP , the government debt/GDP ratio in 2035 would exceed its 2025 level), one possible way to limit the fiscal impact of higher defense spending would be to broaden the scope of what is counted as defense spending ( Figure 6). We think the price rally is overdone, driven by the market’s previous expectation of 2–3 policy-rate cuts from the Fed in 2026 and a materially weaker USD, along with overhyped copper demand from AI data centres . However, we believe data centres account for just 2% of global copper demand and the share will not grow significantly over the next two years (see Data centres update H2 2026 : New hotspots, old constraints, 18 June). Limited downside: We expect the market’s over-estimation of copper demand from data centres to keep supporting copper prices in the near term if optimism on AI continues . The recent US–Iran memorandum of understanding is also likely to boost sentiment on global economic growth and consequently metals demand. We therefore see limited downside from here. Given the expiry of our trade is in mid-July and that prices have risen far above our strikes, option premiums have dropped to near zero and we close our copper put spread at a USD299k loss . Importantly, however, any meaningful supply response is likely to lag given long lead times for new fabs and the strategic focus on advanced-node memory, suggesting that tight conditions could persist in certain segments even as incremental supply comes online. As a result, while further price appreciation is plausible, particularly in higher-performance memory, the trajectory is more likely to shift from sharp step-ups toward a more measured and differentiated trend across product categories. Hyperscalers, some of the largest price-takers in the memory market, continue to attribute rising component costs as a driver of their higher capex forecasts, with memory pricing specifically called out by many. We expect pricing will continue to climb, as demand from both AI and traditional end markets (enterprise/consumer hardware) continues to outstrip available supply. The big three memory producers (Micron, SK Hynix, Samsung) are adding capacity, but given the experience of past cycles, are doing so at a disciplined pace and the timeline for new cleanrooms to come online is long. This suggests that the market will remain very tight in the near term, but begin to moderate gradually in the next 1-2 years as new wafer production comes online. records.text: US Economic Presentation28 June 2026 ab 38 Source: BEA, BLS, Haver, UBS What next? More bumps in the road? The expansion rests on AI and the related wealth gains. We are now at peak fiscal support to growth. We are also at peak tariff impact on inflation and potentially peak energy shock inflation. Will energy prices remain low after the MOU? The labor market appears more vulnerable than appreciated. If the AI investment or support for equities falters, the expansion itself would be at risk. The FOMC will need to confront these risks too, with tensions in the mandate likely leading to tensions in the committee. The distribution of potential outcomes for monetary policy are widening (rates up and down). As a base case, we expect the FOMC would take time before actually enacting rate hikes, and we project the Fed funds rate unchanged in 2026. We are bullish longer term growth and estimate that we are on the cusp of an acceleration in structural growth. Key question(s): Can the geopolitical disruptions, policy uncertainty and volatility get out of the way? However, further upside momentum was missing because there was no catalyst for China rates to rise significantly. The PBoC also started to net inject liquidity a fter interbank rates (e.g., DR001 at 1.50%) had been squeezed modestly above the policy rate of 1.40%. We held the position, believing that downside risk was limited, given that the PBoC is unlikely to revert to the previous excess‑liquidity environment. For gas the picture is similar, with prices close to the March baseline. With that in mind, and given the usual ECB bias, we are not saying a hold in September is unthinkable. In fact, unlike last week after the ceasefire news, a “one and done” is probably now more likely than a third hike. But we would argue that a hold in September would need even lower energy prices or levels not far from where we are today coupled with dovish surprises in the data. Data may not help, here. Short term, the drop in energy prices may actually bring about a sentiment data recovery. Core inflation may be a key factor for the ECB, too. Remember that the persistence of ex-energy inflation was a key argument against cuts a few months ago, Since March, the ECB has been very vocal about concerns that indirect and second-round effects of energy prices would be faster and larger this time. A set of arguments put forth by market participants and the Fed staff suggest the Fed should, at least partly, look through this inflation. First, as detailed above there are potential measurement issues that could be exaggerating the extent of inflation. The second is that it is being driven by industry-specific factors and supply constraints that are beyond the Fed's control, and not a reflection of broader underlying inflation pressures. Indeed, if core PCE ex AI-related categories continues to slow, many think the Fed will be less inclined to set policy to respond to such narrowly concentrated price pressures. In our view, there is some truth to all of these arguments. However, we think it is incorrect to view this AI-related inflation as purely a supply issue. If anything, it is more of a demand problem, with nearly $1 trillion in expected investment chasing various AI-related components. The near-to-medium term trajectory for memory chip prices seems to be higher, or flat at best, with limited potential for a downside amid existing supply chain constraints and profitability incentives for chip producers. This is very different from say, an oil-price shock, which is usually a pure supply-side issue, with an expectation for prices to eventually retreat lower once the constraint is resolved.
