records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 3 Dallas Fed: Output Expands as Employment Strengthens Manufacturing activity remained unchanged in June, according to the Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey. The headline general business activity diffusion index fell 0.4 points to 0 in June, still above its 6-month average of -0.5. Demand and production remained resilient: the production index fell 5.3 points to 4.1 after strong readings in May and April, marking its sixth consecutive month of expansion. The shipments index decreased by 0.3 points, reaching 7.1. The new orders index decreased 4.1 points to 2.3. The moderation of these three indices is not surprising given their strong readings in 2026, we do not take their changes in June as signs of weakness. Labor demand from manufacturers improved strongly. The employment index moved up by 13.7 points to 13.9, while the hours worked index rose to 5.9 from 1.8. Supply chain & inventories: suppliers’ delivery times shortened, with the index down 0.5 points to 0.9. The inventories index improved meaningfully, rising to 7.8 from -12.0. Prices: input prices fell slightly. The prices paid index fell 0.3 points to 42.4, reflecting some of the easing in higher energy prices. Over the last six months, US rates markets have repriced dramatically, with forward rates starting the year implying more than two full cuts by December and now pricing in 31bp of tightening over the same period. With this shift, yields across the curve have risen and the curve has bear flattened: 2-, 5-, 10-, and 30-year yields have risen 62bp, 41bp, 21bp, and 2bp, respectively. Real yields have driven the move, while 5- and 10-year TIPS breakevens are modestly narrower across the curve. On a forward basis, 5Yx5Y inflation swaps have declined by 11bp. The swap spread curve has twist-flattened, with 2-year spreads 2bp wider while 10- and 30-year spreads are 5-6bp narrower. Immediately following the start of the US-Iran conflict at the end of February, bond markets across the DM responded to the energy price shock, with the UK and Germany underperforming, alongside the sharp move in European natural gas prices. We think this was wrongly interpreted to mean that she did not see the need to raise interest rates further. Instead, Lagarde was probably sticking to the framework outlined back in March under which a “measured adjustment” was warranted in response to a “sizeable but not too persistent” shock. Another rate hike (our base case remains for one more in September) would still be consistent with “measured” to the extent that it would leave policy within the ECB’s estimated range (of 1.75% -2.50%) for the neutral interest rate. Executive Board member Isabel Schnab el was even more explicit in a recent interview, saying “we will need to raise interest rates further in order to bring inflation back to our 2% target”. We like to be short 5y5y in Germany, with the trade more fundamentally capturing that July is the year’s second-heaviest month for net supply in this market. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley MUFG 21 Share performance by revenue exposure: A value-oriented stock selection approach is effective for struggling domestic demand stocks We define firms with high revenue exposure to the Americas, DM Europe, China, and Japan as “high exposure stocks” for the relevant regions based on survey data since 2016. The share price performance in absolute terms and in excess returns relative to TOPIX is shown in Exhibit 25 and Exhibit 26 . We set our minimum criteria for high exposure at 20% for the Americas, 15% for both DM Europe and China, and 90% for Japan; these stocks would account for around 20% of the survey’s coverage universe on a company basis. Our domestic high exposure stocks exclude the financial sector. Japanese high exposure stocks generated cumulative negative excess returns of some 60% from July 2016 to June 2026 (Exhibit 26 ). Over the past year in particular they have underperformed TOPIX by around 20%. Overseas demand stocks have been lifted by the recent AI rally, while the yen has weakened from the mid- ¥140/$ range to around ¥160/$ ( Exhibit 27 ), and this has been a headwind for domestic demand stocks with increased import costs. Meanwhile, China high exposure stocks have shown notable outperformance over the year, which we attribute largely to the substantial number of semiconductor- related names in this category. A meaningful erosion of wealth effects could quickly translate into weaker aggregate consumption and labor demand. However, recent experiences tempered this concern. Higher-income spending in BAC data held up during the post Liberation Day equity selloff, suggesting that the cumulative gains in equity markets over recent years have created a sizable buffer. In our view, it typically takes a sustained equity drawdown of 20% or more to generate a material negative wealth effect on spending. Indeed, since the start of the Iran war, higher-income ex gas consumer spending in the BAC data has held up, in large part due to the equity market holding up. And this has sustained as recently as late-June, even after the tax refund buffer is behind us. Downside risk 2: Labor market weakness broadens A second downside risk was that labor income losses among lower-and middle-income households could eventually deepen enough to overwhelm the offset from higher- income consumption. In APxJ and EM, we find over 30% of revenues are derived from foreign markets, with US/Canada the largest at 9% of total, followed by Europe at 5%. Chinese companies are still more heavily dependent on the domestic market, although the foreign revenue share has been rising in recent years and now accounts for 17% of total sales. Outside of China, 51% of EM-ex-China sales are generated abroad, while this figure stands at 56% for APxJ-ex-China, highlighting the importance of the global cycle for the region. EEMEA and LatAm companies also have meaningful global exposure, both standing at 35-37%. Our database shows revenue exposure to different end-markets, i.e. corporates, consumers or government, as well as cost exposure. We find that US companies are the most exposed to consumers, driving almost half of revenues in the region, while European companies are the least exposed to consumers. In terms of corporate spending, European and Japanese companies are the most exposed, with corporates accounting for over 50% of revenues in both regions. records.text: The 21% S&P 500 return over the past 12 months has been driven entirely by n earnings, making the upcoming Q2 2026 reporting season an important catalyst for the forward trajectory of the market. Financials will kick off the Q2 earnings season the week of July 13th, and roughly 75% of S&P 500 market cap will have reported results by the first week of August. While the S&P 500 P/E has recently declined, this week our Sentiment Indicator of equity investor positioning rose to 2.0, the highest reading since December 2024 (Exhibit 24). A solid macro backdrop and the ongoing AI investment boom should lead to n another quarter of strong earnings results despite an elevated hurdle set by analyst estimates. S&P 500 EPS growth registered 17% in Q1, excluding some one-time benefits, which exceeded analyst estimates by 5 percentage points. The consensus forecast for Q2 is for 22% year/year growth. The dispersion of growth expectations across sectors and stocks is wide. AI infrastructure stocks are expected to contribute nearly 60% of S&P 500 EPS growth this quarter, with Micron (MU) and NVIDIA (NVDA) together accounting for more than 40%. Consensus expects the median S&P 500 stock to grow EPS by 9%, but conservative revenue estimates signal upside risk to those forecasts. Relative to Q1, higher energy prices were the primary macro shift that n should affect Q2 results. Recent analyst earnings revisions reflect an expected tailwind for Energy earnings and a headwind to Consumer earnings.

records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear When the Middle East conflict arose, we analysed the impact of past energy supply shocks on FX (see FX: Asia’s sensitivity to supply-driven energy shocks, dated 10 March). We found that USDINR moved with a 0.11 beta to oil – i.e., a 1% rise in oil equated to a 0.11% rise in USDINR. Should oil prices settle around USD80/bbl in 2026, this would represent about a 13% rise from pre- conflict levels. In such a scenario, our analysis would suggest that USDINR should rise by approximately 1.45% from pre-conflict levels, which would put USDINR around 92.30. While we do not expect a return to these levels, especially as we expect US–IN rate differentials to widen due to potential Fed rate hikes (see June FOMC: Every meeting is live, dated 17 June), the study suggests USDINR is embedding some oil risk premium. Scope for INR longs to build: Since the RBI announced measures to attract inflows, the BNP Paribas Global FX Positioning Tracker shows some shift in positioning, with FX investors building INR longs. However, these positions are modest, at a score of +15 (on a +/-50 scale), suggesting scope for longs to build further, which could keep the INR supported (Figure 3). records.text: M Idea Japan Economics | Japan Weaker Headwinds than Previously Expected: CPI Outlook (after June Prelim. Tokyo CPI) Stagflation-like headwinds are likely to be weaker than previously assumed, while our baseline for CPI to move higher YoY from summer remains unchanged. Morgan Stanley MUFG Securities Co., Ltd. Takeshi Yamaguchi Chief Japan Economist Takeshi.Yamaguchi@morganstanleymufg.com +81 3 6836-5404 Masayuki Inui Economist Masayuki.Inui@morganstanleymufg.com +81 3 6836-5407 For important disclosures, refer to the Disclosure Section, located at the end of this report. Key Takeaways Our expectations for CPI rising YoY from summer remain unchanged, but this inflation wave is likely be smaller than in 2022 and 2025. We think cost-push inflation will still be a drag on consumption via weaker real wages in 2H FY2026, but the headwinds will be less strong than previously expected. Expected sharp declines in rice prices are likely to have a non-negligible impact on overall CPI, and could also affect household inflation expectations. records.text: Central banks likely to remain cautious ECB may still deliver second hike How will the ECB react to this inflation picture? The sharp decline in oil prices implies an improved euro area inflation outlook. Even though, at face value, this argues for a less proactive ECB in the near term, a closer assessment may show there are still reasons to hike further. After nearly four months of elevated oil prices, pipeline pressures have already begun to filter beyond the energy complex. And these are likely to keep underlying inflation firm in the quarters ahead, as firms increasingly pass higher costs onto consumers. As highlighted by Chief Economist Lane this week, "while recent progress towards a resolution of the conflict in the Middle East is welcome, uncertainty remains elevated and there are continued risks for inflation to stay above our 2 per cent medium-term target for quite some time" , and "a range of forward-looking signals point to inflationary pressures in the coming months" . In addition, as private consumption and investment recover alongside improving confidence and lower energy prices, demand conditions may turn out stronger than initially anticipated. This could, in turn, encourage firms to pass through costs to selling prices more decisively. We see little evidence of that. Elevated inflation and heightened labour market tightness in 2021, 2022 and early 2023, amplified by administrative decisions – a ~50% increase in the minimum wage between 2019 and 2026 – have driven robust wage growth in the post-Brexit era. But the labour market was largely rebalanced by immigration and, as slack rose, pay pressures subsided. It is important to note that the UK was just one among many DM countries that saw elevated migration flows post-Covid. Those have now subsided in the UK, due partly to government measures, and partly as labour demand has cooled. Given demographic pressures in the EU and CEE countries, it is hard to see how EU migration flows into the UK, even absent Brexit, would have remained as robust into the 2020s as they were between 2004 and 2016. Indeed, EU countries that have seen large immigration flows in recent years, such as Spain, have also largely attracted non-EU migrants. Between 2016 and 2019, as EU migration flows into the UK dropped post-referendum, but as labour demand remained robust, inactive UK workers started returning to the labour market, likely attracted by solid real wage growth (1.75%Y in 2019). records.text: 26 June 2026 US Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 17 Do quarter-end pension flows flatten the curve? Steven Zeng, CFA | Strategist | +1-212-250-9373 Conventional market view suggests that pension and index -related fixed income buying around quarter -end tends to flatten the Treasury curve. We examine the historical evidence. We test this hypothesis using a combination of regression and event analysis. To control for factors that could influence the 10s -30s curve, we first regress the one-day change in 10s -30s on changes in Fed expectations (proxied by the 2y yield), risk sentiment (S&P 500 returns), and oil price changes. These 3 factors are all highly significant, and residuals from the regression thus represent changes in the 10s-30s curve not explained by these macro drivers, for example rebalancing flows. We then analyze these residuals over a 5-day event window surrounding quarter- ends (t -3 to t+1) since 2000. On average, the 10s -30s residual flattened by approximately 0.5bp between t -1 and t0, with the timing consistent with actual observed quarter -end buying. To further assess the impact of rebalancing, we sort quarter -end observations by the size of pension flows (sourced from the Fed’s quarterly flow of funds data), which we then divide by the amount of 20y+ Treasuries outstanding to control for market growth. As today’s chart shows, 10s- 30s flattening is more prominent during periods with above -median and top - quartile pension flows.

Single- asset deals are exposed to concentration risk and tend to price at wider spreads, while workforce housing bonds—serving middle-income tenants—are often non-rated, higher- yielding structures with less reliance on subsidies such as LIHTC (see here). Below, we discuss in some detail GSE-backed muni bonds that provide some of the best credit quality in the multi-housing sector and at times are overlooked by investors, in our view, as they are relatively illiquid and their total outstanding is relatively small. GSEs and tax-exempt financing The GSEs support multifamily housing by reducing funding costs through capital market execution. They provide a credit guarantee on either the loans or the resulting securities, which increases investor demand, thereby resulting in lower borrowing costs. Both Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae have programs in place that works in conjunction with the 4% LIHTC credit, while Ginnie Mae guarantees bonds securitizing LIHTC loans that are insured by the FHA/VA as part of its standard operations. Freddie Mac ML program Freddie Mac issues tax exempt bonds under its ML program. It purchases government notes from its Optigo TAH (Targeted Affordable Housing) lenders and securitizes them. The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications is scheduled to release details of the new expenditure weights on July 10, followed by revised historical CPI estimates for January–June 2025 under the new framework on August 7. The first official nationwide CPI release using the new base year will be published on August 21. We plan to provide forecasts regarding the scale of revisions once the new weighting information becomes available. This event deserves close attention. records.text: 26 June 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 15 Euroland Strategy EGBs Relative Value Corner Ioannis Sokos | Strategist | +44-20-754-75680 Mingyue Xin | Strategist | +44-20-754-10002 The US/Iran deal has so far not led to a sustained compression in EGB spreads. Rather, the average EGB spread is now wider than the level just before the deal was announced. We believe one of the reasons for this is the respective resilience of ECB market pricing, i.e. not following the drop in oil prices. We mentioned that in a recent FICOTD while we entered Dec ECB receivers this week. Further, we've seen some weakness in equities over the past week which also impacted sentiment on EGB spreads. We no longer have enough conviction to forecast hikes in our base case, but it remains a close call. Lower energy prices/a less prolonged energy shock than we previously expected can lower risks of strong second-round effects as long as damage to expectations has not been done already. Because the latter indicators weight all consumers equally, unlike spending. Also, part of the labor slowdown was due to immigration restrictions that had only a limited impact on consumption. We argued last year that as long as higher-income spending, which is more service-oriented, is resilient, labor demand would ultimately stabilize. This is because more than five out of six jobs are in services. The recent pickup in the labor data is consistent with that view. Lessons from the pandemic recovery Pandemic-era fiscal support and excess savings helped fuel a stronger US recovery than the “sluggish” one in Europe. This extended beyond household balance sheets: foreign demand for US assets helped finance large deficits, while strong corporate profitability supported investment and jobs. Over time, large macro shocks interacted with unequal financial buffers and asset gains that, despite broader retail participation in equities, benefited higher-income households, contributing to today's K-shaped consumer. Relative to Q1, higher energy prices were the primary macro shift that should affect Q2 results. Most immediately, higher energy costs are a tailwind for Energy earnings and a headwind to Consumer earnings, and these impulses have been reflected directionally in recent analyst estimate revisions (Exhibit 2). While recent consumer spending data have been strong, our economists expect a slowdown in consumption in the second half of 2026. For Consumer Discretionary stocks, however, the recent decline in oil prices and rebound in consumer sentiment have been more important drivers of short-term volatility. However, even before the war, corporate commentary had signaled increasing input cost pressures, and profit margins will remain a key focus this quarter. Our economists’ company price announcement tracker, which captures both prices paid and received, increased last quarter to its highest level since late 2023, and both PPI inflation and survey measures of supplier delivery times have continued to signal supply chain pressures. Oil prices may fall further in the near term: Since the signing of the MOU by the US and Iran, energy prices have fallen. While in our base case we see the risk of oil prices rising back to USD80/bbl by the end of the year, they remain well below the prices over the past three months. This suggests there should still be some relief on India’s current account balance, a large net energy importer.

Monetary Policy: On hold at 0%, despite ECB rate hikes The SNB kept rates on hold in June with the overall message broadly unchanged from March. It maintained its increased willingness to intervene in FX markets, albeit slightly modified by "if necessary", suggesting interventions are carried out on a discretionary basis rather than continuously - as we have long suspected. Developments since March, including a weaker CHF, have somewhat eased monetary conditions and reduced the need for actual interventions: We estimate that FX purchases were concentrated in March (around CHF 2.5bn), with little meaningful intervention thereafter. Following this modest CHF weakening and due to higher oil price assumptions than in March, the SNB revised its inflation forecast modestly higher across the horizon, but with inflation remaining below the mid-point of the 0 to 2% target range. The upward slope suggests inflation is gradually moving away from very low levels, but the still subdued end-point of 0.8% in 2029 Q1 is not indicating any urgency to tighten policy. The overall message from the June meeting, in our view, is that the SNB is comfortable with its current stance and sees policy as appropriate given still subdued inflation pressures. records.text: US Focus GSE-backed muni housing We discuss GSE-backed muni bonds, which provide some of the best credit quality in the multi-housing sector. This sector might be overlooked by investors, in our view, as it is relatively illiquid and the total outstanding is fairly small. We find that agency CMBS offers attractive relative value. These bonds are supported by credit guarantee from the agency, as well as credit enhancement of at least 5%. • In our view, the large yield pickup is sufficient compensation for the illiquid nature of the bonds, and we think they are appropriate for buy-and-hold municipal investors. • Yields on Freddie ML deals are also attractive compared to after-tax Freddie K A2 bond yields. • Freddie ML is a relatively small market with close to $10bn outstanding, $14bn including the M program. May household inflation expectations This morning the ECB published their CES household inflation expectation data for May (before the MoU between the US and Iran was announced). Median expectations (the ECB's preferred measure) for inflation three years ahead remained unchanged at 2.9% and five-year ahead expectations remained unchanged at 2.4%. But mean (average) inflation expectations eased a bit at both the three and five year horizon. The ECB typically focuses on median expectations over the mean as the open-ended nature of their question structure means that average expectations are biased upwards. However, despite this bias, changes in expectations often have useful predictive power. We also know that the ECB does pay some attention to the signal from average expectations. In a speech in early March, Schnabel sounded a note of concern that despite the progress the ECB had made in bringing down actual inflation, median expectations remained elevated while mean expectations had been creeping up (even before the war). records.text: ab 29 June 2026 Global Research European Economic Comment Germany: The (subdued) view from Berlin Impressions from a macro trip to the German capital Germany's weak growth outlook, structural challenges, the impact of potential reforms and the political outlook dominated our discussions with public officials, think tanks, industry associations and other observers during a two-day client trip to Berlin last week. Compared to past trips, the sentiment was fairly subdued, rooted in the prolonged growth stagnation and perceived lack of reform progress. However, the combination of substantial fiscal stimulus and emerging structural reforms provides potential for cyclical and structural improvement ahead. In fact, most observers expect a growth pick-up into next year. While the period of stagnation should hence come to an end (absent renewed external shocks), most interlocutors stressed that structurally weaker potential growth (~0.5% now vs. ~1.5% in the 2010s) will limit the durability of the recovery. Short-term outlook: fiscal stimulus dominates Most observers agreed on the short-run outlook for GDP growth of around ½% this year and around 1% in 2027 (UBSe: 0.6%/1.5%). Business sentiment remains at multi- year lows, particularly among smaller, domestically-oriented companies. Primary balance to be managed over multiple years At a CEFP meeting on the 25th, PM Takaichi stated that she would position a stable decline in the ratio of central and local government gross debt to GDP as the core of fiscal management, and that the PB would be managed over multiple years. The preparation of a medium-term fiscal plan spanning multiple years is itself an internationally standard measure, and the IMF has long recommended that the Japanese government prepare one. At the CEFP meeting in March this year, Professor Olivier Blanchard also proposed to PM Takaichi that Japan prepare a medium-term fiscal plan of around five years. That said, this is because setting medium-term fiscal targets is meant to encourage fiscal discipline. Monetary Policy: On hold at 0%, despite ECB rate hikes The SNB kept rates on hold in June with the overall message broadly unchanged from March. It maintained its increased willingness to intervene in FX markets, albeit slightly modified by "if necessary", suggesting interventions are carried out on a discretionary basis rather than continuously - as we have long suspected. Developments since March, including a weaker CHF, have somewhat eased monetary conditions and reduced the need for actual interventions: We estimate that FX purchases were concentrated in March (around CHF 2.5bn), with little meaningful intervention thereafter. Following this modest CHF weakening and due to higher oil price assumptions than in March, the SNB revised its inflation forecast modestly higher across the horizon, but with inflation remaining below the mid-point of the 0 to 2% target range. The upward slope suggests inflation is gradually moving away from very low levels, but the still subdued end-point of 0.8% in 2029 Q1 is not indicating any urgency to tighten policy. The overall message from the June meeting, in our view, is that the SNB is comfortable with its current stance and sees policy as appropriate given still subdued inflation pressures. Earnings are, of course, always important for equities, but the earnings context for Asian markets is especially so at present for four reasons. First, the rate of earnings growth and the disparity between different parts of the region is at record levels. We expect 60% and 22% EPS growth for the MXAPJ index in 2026 and 2027, led by Korea (320% and 35% this year and next) and Taiwan (48% and 30%, respectively). In contrast, the ASEAN markets and Australia should post only mid-single digit earnings CAGRs this year and next, with China offshore and India in low double digits. Second, earnings growth explains much of the wide disparity in market performance. Cross-sectional regressions show close to 80% of the ytd performance of regional markets can be explained by earnings growth or revisions to earnings growth forecasts. records.text: M Update 4 CAD Our view: Neutral Risk skew: Bullish Watch: GDP We closed our short USD/CAD recommendation this week, following the hawkish tone struck at the June FOMC. We still think there is room for CAD to recover its recent declines against USD. The USMCA deadline is July 1st. Both the US and Canada have made it clear more time will be needed for negotiations. If negative rhetoric comes from the US administration around the deadline, but there is no real invocation of the 6-month withdrawal clause, we think CAD could benefit from a “kick the can” scenario. We recently hit short CAD levels on MSOPCADU Index that had not been seen since 2023. We have begun to see a technical retracement, and we think there is room to go if April monthly GDP surprises to the upside. Oil and gas had been negative m/m in March. If oil production rose in April or benefits came from elevated Brent prices, we think markets could price hikes in response, and see USD/CAD decline slightly. US CPI is the next clear catalyst for markets, in our view. We think a sustained move lower in USD/CAD rather than just tactical only comes if US CPI surprises to the downside and expectations of US rate hikes are modified. records.text: ds. Ahead of the May local election we noted that risk premiums were already elevated. That remains the case when looking at the cross -market term premium differentials. In fact, the spread between UK and US term premium has reached record levels over the past week, driven largely by the reaction to Fed Governor Warsh’s first press conference. As outlined in this note , we still see scope for higher term premium in the US and have revised forecasts higher due to expected hikes. Term premium tends to co-move, but with the differential already at the wides, we see scope for this to tighten back. We had been arguing the observed risk premium in GBP rates was unlikely to correct substantially given the political uncertainty around leadership challenges. In the near term, the focus will be on the choice of Chancellor, which will also be viewed as a signalling mechanism. Given the economic constraints have not eased, the burden of proof will lie in policy choices. Given the rhetoric so far, it is not obvious that “this time is different”, but valuations already reflect the risk of a fairly sticky deficit trajectory. The immediate fiscal trajectory should matter most for markets, rather than fiscal headroom or other theoretical/forward looking metrics. Deficit expectations have already been worsening. The former likely has further to run (Figure 20), while the latter may be approaching a peak (Figure 21). As a result, we see the risks tilted towards a decline in core goods inflation in June. Looking further ahead, indirect effects from higher commodity costs are still expected to lead to an acceleration in H2 this year. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Notably, the DMO has not yet issued any long conventional gilts. The July calendar includes only one long tender, previously expected to be auctioned, ahead of a potential long conventional syndication in September (see Exhibit 10 ). While the current financing remit states “one or more new and/or existing medium and/or long conventional gilts,” we expect a long syndication. Our base case is for a new 20y conventional gilt, likely sized in the £5bn–£6bn range, potentially in the week commencing 14 September 2026. Consultation meetings suggested either a reopening of the 5Q41 or the launch of a new 20y conventional gilt. Given the absence of long issuance so far this fiscal year, we believe a long syndication remains the most likely outcome. The July calendar is relatively light, consisting of a 5y linker auction, the 10y green gilt auction, a 10y conventional gilt auction a 3y conventional gilt auction, three planned tenders, one of which is scheduled in the long end, and the linker syndication. The DMO has since announced that the syndication will be a tap of the IL38, scheduled for the week commencing 13 July 2026. Low July supply should be supportive for carry trades over the next month. That said, it is important to flag that both the geopolitical and domestic backdrops remain uncertain and may keep realized volatility elevated over the summer. They also suggest that changes in pricing strategies by software companies makes it more challenging to measure a pure price increase. The authors also make other arguments highlighting mis-measurement, such as the misalignment of the subcomponents that make up "Computer software and accessories" in the CPI and PCE price indices, and the gaping difference in category weights. They conclude that a quarter to well over a half of the contribution of this category to core PCE may be an outcome of these measurement errors combined. Indeed, the BEA announced late last week that it plans to address some of the measurement concerns in this category in its upcoming annual update in September (more on this below). While we agree that computer software needs quality adjustment and is probably overstating inflation currently, we also think the surge in the "accessories" component is truly a reflection of AI-related demand rapidly depleting industry inventories, and with limited quality adjustment issues here, it makes us more inclined to view these price increases as "real" . Another glaring difference is the weight for this category in the PCE versus the CPI index. records.text: 26 June 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 9 US Rates Strategy Update Incorporating Fed hikes into the rates forecast Matthew Raskin | Strategist | +1-212-250-1741 Steven Zeng, CFA | Strategist | +1-212-250-9373 Andrew Fu | Strategist | +1-212-250-1743 Note: This note was originally published on 23 June 2026. Following last week’s FOMC meeting, our economists updated their Fed outlook. They now expect two 25bp hikes this year, in September and December, bringing the fed funds rate to 4.1%. The forecast then has the Fed on hold throughout 2027 before returning policy to our estimate of long-run neutral (3.5-3.75%) in 2028. We are revising our SOFR swap and Treasury rate forecasts in line with that updated policy path. We maintain all other assumptions from our prior forecast – namely, a nominal neutral rate of 3.5 -3.75%, increases in term premia driven primarily by rising bond supply held by price -sensitive investors, and a modest widening in swap spreads (i.e., relative richening in USTs) due to benign funding conditions and a supportive regulatory backdrop. The tables below detail the updated projection. The revision lifts our front -end forecasts – with 2y UST at 4.3% at year-end (+35bps vs. prior) – but has a muted impact on longer-term yields given the assumption that hikes are rolled back by mid-2028. We now have 10y UST at 4.8% at year-end (+10bps vs. prior). Relative to market forwards, the projection has in-line front-end rates but steeper curves.

However, for that to happen, we believe strong and sustained pass-through from more sticky wages to prices would be essential. Economics Europe Blog Date 26 June 2026 Flash June HICP preview Flash inflation releases for June begin on Monday (29 Jun) , with Spain and Belgium reporting first. France, Germany and Italy follow on Tuesday (30 Jun), before the euro area aggregate on Wednesday (1 Jul). We see headline HICP easing to 2.95% YoY (3.17% prev.) as energy HICP declines following the recent correction in commodity prices. This is broadly in line with current market pricing and slightly lower than consensus. We also see core HICP easing slightly, to 2.5% YoY (2.6% prev.), as moderate underlying services pressure and a temporary drag from clothing offset continued strength in airfares. For the ECB, the recent oil correction reduces the pressure for a more aggressive policy response. The energy shock might have peaked, but the ECB is likely to remain focused on any signs of a broader pass-through from higher energy costs. Inflation persistence risks have not fully disappeared. This continues to support the case for a ‘measured’ tightening response and a second and final rate hike in September. Maria Contreras Economist +44-20-754-74120 Mark Wall Ch

records.text: US Economic Presentation28 June 2026 ab 14 Source: Census, USATRADE, Haver, UBS • The Supreme Court struck down the tariffs imposed under IEEPA. The administration has moved quickly to deploy a blanket section 122 tariff of 10%. Without Congressional approval, those tariffs are set to expire July 24, 2026. • The administration appears to be working on a “plan B” , recently announcing findings in a section 301 investigation covering 60 trade partners. Using section 301, if the administration replicates the IEEPA tariffs for just the top 10 trading partners, the WATR would return close to the pre-ruling level. Section 301 has withstood legal challenge, but the new actions could still be challenged in the courts. • A refund process for the approximately $160bn paid in IEEPA tariffs is now established. Only certain importers are eligible initially and the process is complex. This likely means a long, drawn-out process and refunds will flow to larger importers, who are less likely to spend them. records.text: US Focus NAIC CLO proposal finalized with unexpectedly broader applicability The NAIC Working Group voted to approve the updated RBC factors with a few tweaks, most notably that the new factors will also apply to PC CLOs, CDOs, and CBOs. This regulatory change will affect about $260bn of securities owned by life insurers, likely effective for YE26 reporting. This is a reprint of US Insurance and CLOs: On the CLOck: NAIC CLO Proposal Finalized with Unexpectedly Broader Applicability, published on June 25, 2026. However, on June 24 Reuters reported that the government is considering improvements in the way the assets of the Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account are managed, and some of the returns could be a possible funding source. While it is appropriate to effectively utilize existing assets, in that case there would be a need to dispose of Treasuries, which are thought to account for the bulk of assets. One option would be to lengthen duration, but this would hardly constitute an improvement in asset management. If it were to provide additional returns sufficient to fund fiscal policy, this asset management would need to be on a considerable scale. Obtaining the approval of the US would be an issue. At the Japan Growth Strategy Council, one member expressed concern that growth in pension funds has absorbed long-term funds and around 50% is allocated to overseas investments. Within the context of monetary policy and the rise in long- term interest rates, one way to correct this would be to return GPIF asset management to JGBs. It would be possible to increase the weighting given that interest rates have risen. However, the current portfolio allocation is determined by expected returns, and to change it would require considerable work. At current JGB yields it would not be possible to sustainably achieve the target of 2% plus the rate of increase in wages.

FDI data are as complex as trade data, but they offer little evidence of an immediate post-Brexit underperformance. FDI inflows slowed down in 2024 and 2025, but that looks to have been part of a more global trend. The decline in inward FDI flows looks comparable to that seen in Germany and France. It is important to note that, while business capex was weak during the immediate post- referendum period, in recent years, it has outperformed overall GDP growth. A combination of sectoral, expenditure and survey data points to a decent capex boost to UK growth over 2025, with AI adoption likely one of the key drivers. Clean energy transition is also fairly visible in the capex data, and is a structural capex tailwind that is likely to persist in the near term. All in all, we do think the economy is shifting from low capex/low productivity growth towards a better equilibrium – albeit at a slow pace capped by still elevated policy uncertainty and high financing costs.

records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 29 Jun 2026 09:37:23 ET │ 15 pages US Economics Inflation Weekly – BEA to change methodology for important PCE components CITI'S TAKE Core PCE rose 0.32%MoM in May, softer than the 0.37% we had been penciling in but with some upward revisions to previous months that kept the year-on-year reading climbing to 3.4%. But the most important development last week was an announcement by the BEA that they will be changing the methodologies for some important components of PCE prices, including computer software and accessories, legal services, and portfolio management services. There is still substantial uncertainty around these methodology changes, with revisions introduced in the September 30 GDP/PCE release. But for now, we estimate that the new methodologies will have the effect of lowering year-on-year core PCE by around 25bp. This would put our current tracking of 3.1% Q4/Q4 core PCE closer to 2.8%, half a percentage point below the Fed’s median 3.3% forecast. Since the program's inauguration in 2017, Freddie Mac has issued close to $10bn in ML bonds. Deals are typically structured with a senior tranche that is sold through syndication and a junior tranche that is either retained by the sponsor or sold separately. The junior tranche provides a 5% to 10% credit enhancement to class-A investors. Freddie Mac guarantees timely principal and interest on the senior tranche, while the junior tranche is not guaranteed. (Figure 3) Compared to the more common 5- and 10-year Freddie K deals, these deals tend to offer longer WALs, reaching 10 to 15 years. records.text: US Economic Viewpoint | 29 June 2026 3 Is the K starting to close? More recently, BAC aggregated debit and credit card data for the first half of June show the gap in total card spending ex-gas between higher- and lower-income households narrowing (Exhibit 1). Alongside this, a recent Bank of America Institute report showed a rise in after-tax wage growth for lower- and middle- income households. It is still too early to confirm a sustained shift, as the recent improvement could partly reflect tax relief, but the data bear watching. However, if this narrowing of the K is sustained, one explanation could be job growth broadening into more blue-collar sectors such as leisure & hospitality, construction and manufacturing. Recent data provide some tentative evidence of this, alongside an improvement in professional & business services hiring after job losses throughout '25, which disproportionately affected younger, lower- income workers. Potential drivers could be reduced tariff uncertainty, ongoing equity market strength, and consequently robust higher-income spending. This would be consistent with the pre-K environment. Before the K-shaped consumer emerged in late-'24/early-'25, lower-income households saw faster spending and wage growth than higher-income households, reflecting a labor market led by blue-collar industries such as leisure & hospitality. records.text: he Strait of Hormuz having lasted nearly four months, pipeline pressures have already begun to filter beyond the energy complex and are likely to keep underlying inflation firm in the quarters ahead, as firms increasingly pass higher costs onto consumers. As highlighted by Chief Economist Lane this week, "while recent progress towards a resolution of the conflict in the Middle East is welcome, uncertainty remains elevated and there are continued risks for inflation to stay above our 2 per cent medium-term target for quite some time" , and "a range of forward-looking signals point to inflationary pressures in the coming months" . In addition, as private consumption and investment recover alongside improving confidence and lower energy prices, demand conditions may turn out stronger than initially anticipated. This could, in turn, encourage firms to pass through costs to selling prices more decisively. In other words, even if the initial shock proves smaller than previously assumed, the transmission to the broader economy may strengthen as demand catches up – a point also made by Executive Board member Schnabel in her interview with Die Zeit: "the recent fall in oil prices may make it easier for companies to pass on past cost increases to consumers, as demand is likely to pick up again. Performance for the ROE factor has been trending down since 2021, implying that low- ROE stocks are outperforming high-ROE stocks. This is because the economic risk of some CLOs is ceded to reinsurers through asset-intensive reinsurance, even if the regulatory accounting does not reflect that. In those cases, the life insurer will report CLOs in their portfolio, even though the economic risk of the asset is transferred to the reinsurer (see Insurance Perspectives: Being Transparent about Transparency). As a result, the NAIC's risk weights (current and proposed) may not apply to all the CLO holdings shown in Schedule D of the life buying the reinsurance. This asymmetry makes a systematic analysis of the effects of this proposal impossible to complete without risking over-stating the potential drag on RBC ratios. This is because many insurers have put lower-rated CLOs into funds withheld reinsurance agreements, thereby shielding them from the higher risk weights. Therefore, in our analysis, we have quantified the direct exposure of Latin American corporates by their underlying demand source. For example, beverage manufacturer Ambev sells its products to wholesale and retail companies, which in turn sell the products to individuals. Thus, from the perspective of Ambev, we considered the company’s clients to be individuals. Our key conclusions are: • Corporations represent 48% of total revenues. Furthermore, a sector breakdown indicates Energy, Information Technology, Materials and Real Estate companies have the highest exposure to corporates. • Consumers produce 52% of total revenues. Utilities and Industrials have the highest exposure to government revenues.

Looking through the details, much of May's firming (+10bp) reflected the anticipated rebound in financial services, with the re-ascent of equity prices in recent months feeding through to portfolio management fees and commissions. With equities having retraced some of those gains, this impulse should fade in June, providing some mechanical relief to monthly inflation. By contrast, the "computer software and accessories" category, which includes memory products (RAM chips and external SSDs) and other items sensitive to the AI capex boom, leveled in May following a series of robust monthly increases. Even so, we are skeptical this represents the new run rate, with pipeline indicators still pointing to underlying price pressures for these components. Besides this, unexpected deflation in the "nonprofit institutions serving households" component was a meaningful offset in May, from which we would infer little signal. Putting the pieces together, we expect core PCE inflation to soften in June to a pace rounding down to 0.2% m/m, with the partial unwind of financial services doing much of the heavy lifting. Even so, one should resist over-interpreting any short-term improvements, with base effects alone likely to keep year-over-year inflation at or slightly above 3% through the remainder of the year. records.text: US Credit Alpha Overview Spreads remained resilient, especially for investment grade, even as supply continued to run hot and equity volatility picked up. Strong fundamentals should help keep spreads range-bound near recent tights. No lack of supply Spreads were slightly wider this week, with investment grade outperforming high yield in cash. After trading in a tight 1bp range for the past month (72-73bp), the IG cash index reached one-month wides of 74bp on Wednesday, which normally would not be notable except for the lack of movement over the prior month. The spread widening coincided with a sharp rally in Treasuries on Wednesday as rates declined sharply across the curve. High yield fared comparatively worse, as spreads were 12bp wider for the week as of Wednesday's close and are now the widest (277bp) since mid-April, with the weakness driven largely by CCCs. The HY/IG spread ratio is now at eight-month highs (Figure 2). In contrast to credit, equity markets were volatile, as the Mag 7 underperformed significantly amid continued AI capex concerns while healthcare and utilities outperformed. Semiconductor stocks, which were in focus ahead of and following Micron earnings (which exceeded expectations)and segments of the leveraged ETF market were particularly volatile. The SOX traded in a 10% range and was down 3% for the week as of midday Thursday. Prime Minister Keir Starmer resigns On Monday morning, Keir Starmer announced his resignation as prime minister. He set out a timetable for an orderly transition of power to a new prime minister, one that would see nominations open from 9-16 July and, if a contest is to take place, the new leader would be in position at the beginning of September (see First Look: Prime Minister Starmer resigns, 22 June 2026). However, our base case is for the process to be uncontested, with almost all of the possible candidates declaring their support for newly elected MP Andy Burnham. It therefore appears highly probable that Burnham could be announced as Labour leader and PM by 17 July. What do we know about Burnham's policy agenda? There has been relatively little concrete information, beyond what we have already written about. We understand there will be a speech next week, likely Monday, which we expect to be aimed at giving more detail (although still remaining high level) and reassuring markets. Therefore, we expect it to reaffirm commitment to the fiscal rules in their current form, which would leave little room for other policies, especially with the added pressure of increased defence spending requirements, and Burnham's commitment to manifesto pledges to not increase income tax, national insurance or VAT . records.text: European Equity Strategy29 June 2026 ab 12 Switzerland's Economic Outlook 2026-27 Inflation: Modest pickup, but only due to energy Inflation remained unchanged at 0.6% y/y in May and is still largely driven by energy. This is likely the peak of the energy-driven increase for now, with inflation expected to hover around 0.5% throughout the summer before picking up moderately to around 1% in Q4. Inflation pressures are expected to remain contained because of offsetting forces from a still strong CHF, Switzerland’s lower energy weight in the CPI and limited risks of second-round inflation via wages amid a weakened labour market. Overall, we expect inflation to average 0.5% in 2026 and 0.7% in 2027/28. Growth: Through the trough, but return to trend growth only next year After just 0.2% q/q growth in Q4 and a contraction in Q3 '25, the Swiss economy expanded strongly in Q1 '26, growing 0.7% q/q. This was partly boosted by licensing income from the Winter Olympics but also by solid manufacturing activity, which benefitted from catch-up effects after last year’s high US tariffs. Meanwhile, private consumption stagnated in Q1. Going forward, we are sceptical how long the modest manufacturing recovery can last in light of the energy shock and expect industrial momentum to weaken from here, so that overall growth will likely run somewhat below trend in coming quarters. records.text: Even with gasoline prices having slid about 15% from their peak in early June, income fundamentals remain very soft, to our eye. Although both personal and disposable income showed strong 0.7% m/m increases in May ( Figure 4), much of this reflects idiosyncratic swings in nonwage components, including farm price supports from the American Relief Act (2025), which are approaching their endpoint. By contrast, the trajectory of labor compensation— which tends to be more reliable metric of underlying income trends—points to ongoing purchasing power challenges despite the recent pickup in job gains, having risen at an average pace of 0.4% m/m from March-May, somewhat slower than the pace of PCE price inflation. This makes it difficult for us to infer a clean step-up in household spending fundamentals that would sustain Q2's spending pickup. Given this, we retain our outlook that the pace of consumer spending will settle at about 1.5% q/q saar in H2 2026, taking some signal from the improvements in purchasing power implied by recent oil price developments, but fading the strong spending signals during Q2. As we move into the summer period, carry-and-roll trades should become more relevant, supported by seasonally lower realized volatility and lighter supply. Our cross-market screen highlights three key opportunities: front-end gilt ASW wideners, especially 3y and 7y, offer the strongest carry per unit of volatility; in SONIA, the cleanest outright carry is in the 10y–15y spot sector and in belly/intermediate forwards such as 5y5y and 4y2y; and among relative-value structures, receiver flies still screen well on C&R/Vol, while long-end steepeners such as 5y5y/10y10y and 10y10y/20y10y are supported by both carry and July seasonality. That said, entry levels are mixed, and geopolitical and domestic risks may keep realized volatility elevated through the summer. The impact on total JGB issuance is, of course, likely to be even greater after also factoring in the aforementioned “bridging bond” issuance under a separately managed special account. The government has indicated that for fiscal management purposes it will be targeting steady reductions in the debt-to-GDP ratio over time, implying an assumption that growth in outstanding debt will be outpaced by growth in nominal GDP. However, even the Cabinet Office’s simulations show a risk of that ratio starting to rise from FY2030 under the “projection of past trend” scenario where the demand will increase only to the extent of the additional fiscal spending amount (i.e., government’s growth strategy fails to stimulate private-sector capital investment) (see Exhibit 5 ). It suggests to us that overseas investors might very well be skeptical of a fiscal management approach that rests so heavily on the assumption of (by no means certain) accelerations in future growth. Multifamily housing municipal bonds encompass a range of structures that vary primarily by their credit support and underlying collateral. In general, we break multi-family housing issuance down into several distinct segments: GSE-backed; Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC)-backed private activity bonds (PABs) with GSE collateral; non-agency deals (both LIHTC and non LIHTC); and private placements. Bonds issued by state or local housing finance agencies are typically secured by large, diversified pools of mortgage loans and generally carry strong credit ratings. These transactions may also benefit from supplemental credit support, such as FHA mortgage insurance, GNMA- guaranteed mortgage-backed securities, or credit enhancement from Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. In contrast, multifamily housing projects can also be financed on a single-asset basis, where credit risk is concentrated at the property level. GSE-backed multifamily munis primarily benefit from explicit GSE guarantees at the bond level, where Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac typically also contractually back the underlying mortgage. It is worth noting that the LIHTC is a federal program that supports affordable rental housing by converting future tax credits into upfront equity. We believe the 100+bp pickup in yield is sufficient compensation for the illiquid nature of ML bonds, and think they are appropriate for buy-and-hold municipal investors. For comparison, the more liquid traditional multifamily muni housing bonds backed by Fannie and Freddie collateral typically provide spread pickup of 40-60bp over the AAA tax-exempt curve. In our view, the main reason for this cheapness is that tax-sensitive investors are not fully familiar with these structures. Yields on Freddie ML senior tranches are also attractive compared with after-tax Freddie K A2 bond yields. Class A of the most recent ML deal, priced at the start of the month, was issued at a 4.4% yield with a 14y WAL, while class A2 of the most recent 10y Freddie K bond was priced at 4.8%, which equates to a 3.8% post-tax yield (here we used the top corporate tax bracket of 21%; for retail investors in the 37% tax bracket, these bonds provide an even more attractive spread pickup) (Figure 6). Of note, the WAL for Freddie K deals is typically 10 years, compared with Freddie ML bonds which have a higher WAL of up to 15 years. Figure 10 shows that the 2026 distribution has moved away from last year’s pattern, with more industrial long-end issuance and less concentration in shorter industrial and utility maturities. However, Figure 11 makes the more important point: compared with the 10-year average, 2026 does not look especially unusual. It is 2025 that looks like the outlier. A very uneven issuance distribution, and spreads are noticing The increase in issuance has been very uneven across sectors. Gross issuance has grown very quickly in a few sectors while remaining much more subdued elsewhere. Tech & AI-related issuers have been the clearest outliers. Now that this gap has narrowed, the choice of being short 10y rather than 1y1y is in fact better aligned with the underlying fundamental drivers behind our view. Indeed, the next challenge to overcome is the apparent reluctance of the market to fully price the shift in the supply/demand of bonds (as captured by our free float metric) into term premia. Unlike the front-end, the term premium tends to reprice slowly over several years rather than quickly in a matter of weeks. Moreover, seasonal patterns have historically proved to be a headwind in the summer months. Thus, this next challenge is unlikely to be resolved swiftly. Still, it is worth reiterating the key factors supporting the higher term premia view. The starting point is that the term premium, as we define it, remains close to its historical lows if we exclude the 2014/21 period dominated by the positive supply shock from shale oil and the oversized QE during Covid. Absent new positive supply shocks, the conditions prevailing during this period are not present today. records.text: TRADE IDEA TRADE IDEA 26/06/2026 1 EM rates: Closing our 2y Camara payer We close our 2y Camara payer position as it has touched its stop-loss level, booking a loss of 42.5bp (USD425k). We exited after the Camara curve was repriced lower—a move driven by a rally in core rates, weak Chilean activity and inflation data, and declining oil prices. Moreover, the June monetary-policy report (IPoM) from the BCCh reiterated the market’s view that no rate hikes are expected in the foreseeable future. From a multi-month perspective, we still think the market is overlooking the possibility of the BCCh tightening due to second-order inflation impacts linked to the conflict- driven spike in oil prices and the potential for Fed rate rises as soon as December (for our base case, see US: Changing our Fed call to rate hikes, dated 5 June). To recap, we opened the 2y Camara payer (switching from a Camara-US spread payer) on 1 June in the belief that the existing hiking premium was modest compared with upside inflation risks. We also expected the June IPoM to serve as a pivotal catalyst that could lead the market to price in additional hiking premium (see EM rates: Switching into outright 2y Camara payer). records.text: ab 26 June 2026 Global Research Japan Macro Watch Fiscal ambitions constrained by market confidence Fiscal update: Bold vision, cautious communication This week, the government announced a plan to mobilize over ¥370tn in public and private investment across 17 strategic sectors by 2040, including ¥10.5tn for Physical AI, ¥24.5tn for gaming, and ¥32.7tn for data centers and batteries. Equity markets responded positively, raising expectations for a government-led growth strategy. However, the government did not disclose the amount of fiscal spending or JGB issuance associated with the plan, leaving its fiscal implications unclear. While the ¥370tn headline is ambitious, the lack of concrete funding details also reflects concern over rising interest-rate risks. According to Minister Katayama, next year's bond issuance will be determined during the budget process after assessing economic and revenue conditions while preserving market confidence, suggesting an approach guided by ongoing dialogue with markets. The caution is understandable. This year's Basic Policy shifts the fiscal objective from achieving a primary balance surplus to reducing the debt-to-GDP ratio, making nominal growth and interest rates as important as the primary balance. Without maintaining market confidence, the scope for a more expansionary fiscal stance remains limited. The company cited an "extraordinary surge in demand for memory" and unprecedented cost inflation,7 which was particularly notable given that Apple has historically raised device prices alongside new model launches rather than in response to discrete input-cost pressure. HPQ has flagged sequential increases in memory costs, with further pressure expected through the second half, and acknowledged this as a key driver of margin headwinds in its PC segment. The company’s response has been to reprice and shift its mix toward higher-end devices, with strength in premium categories and AI PCs helping to offset weaker unit volumes. Figure 19 shows this dynamic more broadly, with derived PC ASPs moving higher across both HPQ and DELL; Dell’s higher absolute ASP primarily reflects its heavier commercial / enterprise client mix, while HPQ’s broader consumer and channel exposure weighs on its blended ASP . In effect, rising memory costs are accelerating a mix-driven strategy across the PC market, where higher-ASP configurations become the primary lever to sustain margins. records.text: GCP/capex/other: $40-55bn in FY26, versus prior FY26 forecast of $25-35bn There has been $16bn of GCP/capex issuance so far in 1H26, and we expect another $24-39bn in 2H26, for a FY26 forecast of $40-55bn. Although this category is difficult to forecast, we project a higher volume and wider range in 2H26 due to anticipated AI infrastructure build outs, including some potential debut issuers to the high yield market (see Tracking Issuance Across Asset Classes). A note on seasonality The midpoint of our forecast implies that ~56% of full-year issuance will occur in 2H. While this would make 2026 a more backend-loaded year than usual, we consider this plausible. 1H issuance likely understated full-year funding demand because geopolitical volatility and shifting Fed expectations created an uncertain issuance environment. With refinancing needs still substantial, we think some supply was delayed, leaving room for a heavier 2H. While most years see less than half of annual issuance occur in the second half, a backend-loaded year is not unprecedented; 2006, 2009, 2010, 2012, 2019, 2020, and 2025 also had more than 50% of issuance come after June (Figure 17). As we recently argued , the repricing in Fed expectations has brought front -end USD rates broadly in line with our t op-down assessment of neutral . At the same time, US data surprise indicators and equity markets have moved off their highs. On the inflation side, market pricing is relatively benign: 2y USD CPI is currently just above 2.30%, pointing to US inflation expectations broadly at target over the next two years, while forwards such as 2y1y are at the low end of their 1y range. Meanwhile, macro factors continue to support higher term premia, particularly in real rates (see here). Against this backdrop, we see scope for a steeper USD 2s10s real yield curve, which inverted this week (Figure left). A rise in inflation pricing would tend to benefit this spread (Figure right), as would a steepening in the nominal curve. The key risk to the trade is a further decline in oil prices, which would mechanically steepen the USD CPI curve while having a more limited impact on the nominal curve. Business services and travel have been particularly strong drivers of services exports growth, with the US accounting for a higher market share among UK services sector corporates. However, it is important to note that it is challenging to separate any post-Brexit structural shifts from the cyclical pull of the robust US economy – a global DM outperformer – in recent years. Indeed, our bias is to assume the outperformance of the UK's services sector is largely a cyclical story. Summing all this up, we note that the hit to UK trade materialised post-Brexit, albeit with some caveats. The UK underperformed its G7 peers in trade volumes – where trade openness as a metric combines both imports and exports – after the TCA came into force in 2021. However, by 2025 trade openness had rebounded back towards the G7 average, supported by strong services exports. Given the potentially cyclical nature of the services exports outperformance, one can look at UK trade openness in the counter-factual space. Had the UK's goods trade openness fared in line with G7 peers, the strength of its services exports would have meant that the UK would have outperformed the G7 average by almost 4pp in terms of overall trade openness by 2025.

Moreover, we think synthetic studies of this kind, by design, work better over a very short period in the immediate aftermath of the shock. The more time passes after a shock materialises, the more variation there is in how economies evolve. The curious case of Northern Ireland: One can instead turn to Northern Ireland, which occupies a unique position in post-Brexit UK. Although it left the EU alongside the rest of the UK, Northern Ireland remains in the EU single market for goods, as both the UK and the EU needed to agree to an arrangement that would not disrupt the Good Friday Agreement and the common travel area on the island of Ireland. We leverage this institutional difference by employing a synthetic difference-in-differences approach using UK regions, which helps mitigate the weakness of cross-country comparisons. The drawback of this approach, however, is the quality of regional data in the UK, which is subpar. We create a doppelgänger Northern Ireland as a weighted sum of other UK regions – namely the North East (47%), West Midlands (13%) and Wales (40%). Using 2016 as the intervention date, we observe a 3% difference in GVA by 2023 for the doppelgänger mix of other UK regions relative to Northern Ireland. The spread signal is calculated as the ratio of the current spread relative to the prior one-year median spread. The values are then smoothed using a 20-day moving average. For example, a multiple of 1 indicates that the current average spread is equal to the historical median spread for that currency pair, whereas a multiple reading of 2 indicates that the current average spread for that given currency pair is twice as wide as its historical median. Turbulence is a price-based measure of the joint unusualness of G10 currency returns. It captures spikes in volatility in individual market components as well as correlation breakdowns – atypical co-movements – between these components. records.text: tronger growth in the coming months, output prices could prove stickier than implied by the normalisation in input costs, as firms gain pricing power and pass through the cumulative cost increases incurred over recent months. On prices, in the UK, composite input price slowed to 70.6 by 4.1pt, split evenly between manufacturing and services. The composite output price index decelerated to 60.1 (-1.5pt), with less inflationary pressure in both services (59.1, -1.5pt) and manufacturing (66.3, -1.7pt). This represents the second month in a row that price indices have eased, after rising significantly in March and April. While they remain above their long-run averages, this likely reflects easing energy prices and we think this is tentatively supportive of the more muted indirect energy effects that we have taken from official price data. The week also brought in the the June vintage of the Citi/YouGov inflation expectations survey, which showed that the one-year-ahead and the longer-term horizon inflation expectations fell to 3.8% y/y (-0.9pp) and to 3.9% y/y (-0.1pp), respectively. These series now sit in line with their Q4 25 averages, and have retreated considerably since their increases at the start of the Middle East conflict. The reading should give some relief to members of the MPC that inflation expectations have not continued to accelerate after the initial energy price shock and remain relatively anchored. Key Takeaways We survey and analyze the exposure of nearly 500 Japanese firms in our coverage universe to certain regions and countries worldwide. These firms have overseas revenue exposure of 40-50%. The ratio has gradually increased even at non-manufacturers in recent years. In terms of share price performance, domestic demand stocks have underperformed over the past year, reflecting yen depreciation and the AI rally. Within the domestic demand stock universe, factor return dynamics differ from those of the broader market. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 226/06/2026 Our base case is for the Fed to raise rates three times in succession, starting in December (see US: Changing our Fed call to rate hikes, dated 6 June). Tactically, we see two scenarios developing in the coming weeks: Scenario 1 – later and longer: In this scenario, the Fed delays hiking for a few months. records.text: M Idea 2 10 Years On from the Referendum – What Have We Learnt? Bruna Skarica What did we think back then? In September 2019, our trade modelling suggested a (front-loaded) 2% hit to UK GDP in case of a "no deal" Brexit outcome, as the UK economy adjusted to increased EU trade frictions. A number of studies between 2016 and 2020 aimed to estimate the near- and medium-term impact of Brexit. The Trade and Cooperation Agreement UK and the EU reached at the very end of 2020 was at the time described as "hard Brexit". While it did not default UK's trade arrangements with the EU back to WTO rules (i.e. it is a a no-tariff, no-quota agreement for trade in goods), it has kept Great Britain out of the EU's customs union and the single market, which has resulted in an increase in non-tariff trade barriers. The most apt approximation of what the assumed impact of the TCA would be, were, thus, various trade modelling studies of a "no deal" or "hard Brexit". We outline a selection of these in Exhibit 1. The medium-term GDP hit from a hard/no deal Brexit as estimated by academics, think tanks, UK and international policy institutions ranged from ~3% to as high as 10%. The transmission channels were broadly consistent across these studies: for one, it was assumed that reduced access to the EU market would lower trade openness and foreign direct investment, which would lead to lower productivity growth. records.text: tat, Morgan Stanley Research What next? Ten years after the referendum, YouGov surveys show that just under 60% of Britons think the UK was wrong to vote to leave the EU, including 23% of Leave voters. While 55% of Britons say they support the UK rejoining the EU, this falls to just 35% if the UK had to rejoin without its prior opt-outs. Still, the Labour government campaigned in 2024 on improving the UK relations with the EU. The UK-EU summit scheduled for July 22 was meant to be the first material step forward, with talks on the Youth Experience Scheme, the common sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) area, and linking the UK and EU emissions trading systems. The SPS deal was meant to remove border checks for EU-GB agri-food trade, allowing dynamic alignment between the UK and EU – whereby the UK would keep in step with the relevant EU SPS/food rules over time. However, in light of Prime Minister Starmer's resignation, the two sides have put the timing of the summit under review. Our assumption is that the new Prime Minister will follow similar policies on attempting to improve on the parts of the Trade and Cooperation Agreement.

records.text: Brexit on the UK economy? Several academic studies (e.g. Springford (2022), Bloom et al. (2025)) have employed a synthetic difference- in-differences approach to estimating the impact of Brexit. For example, Springford (2022) matches the UK to a basket of countries using several pre-Brexit variables, such as real GDP, inflation, services and goods trade. This synthetic economy is then used to estimate how the UK might have performed post-2016 in the absence of Brexit. These studies find a GDP loss of around 5-8% attributable to Brexit since 2016. We do think, however, that one ought to be careful with doppelgänger studies. Brexit coincided with a number of shocks – the Covid pandemic and the surge in energy prices in the EU and UK, to name but two. Hence, isolating the impact of Brexit alone is challenging in a cross-country context. An alternative approach is to look at Northern Ireland, which remains in the EU single market for goods but has otherwise seen the same shocks as other UK regions. We leverage this institutional difference by employing a synthetic difference-in-differences approach using UK regional data, and observe a 3% delta in GVA by 2023 for the UK doppelgänger regions relative to Northern Ireland. This is around half of the hit found in other cross-country synthetic studies, and seems more in line with the OBR's 4% long-run hit estimate. records.text: Wireless services case study: When quality adjustment rewrote the code The CPI category "wireless telephone services" has had two episodes of a discrete downward shift in the index value. In March 2017, the index fell 7% m/m as a carrier shift to unlimited data plans interacted with BLS’s then-existing quality-adjustment methods. In December 2025, the 3% m/m drop was tied to an explicit BLS methodology change, replacing survey pricing with secondary plan data and hedonic/Törnqvist methods. The 2017 episode drew criticism from analysts, because the BLS effectively treated the representative consumer as if they immediately switched to the new plans, thereby exaggerating deflation. In reality, only a subset of users (those changing contracts) benefited right away. To address this somewhat crude quality-adjustment method, the BLS introduced methodology and source changes in 2025, which also had the effect of depressing wireless services prices. It is plausible that the "Computer software & accessories" PCE category, which currently has no quality adjustment, could also undergo a discrete quality adjustment in future that could end up wiping out all the inflation we are seeing today. Th e blue vertical line is drawn in August 2003, when the Fed began to provide forward guidance on the fed funds rate in some form. (Under Greenspan this was qualitative, with language like “measured pace”; over time and especially post-GFC it became much more concrete.) What stands out is that surprises to the current policy target have been substantially smaller since the Fed began using forward guidance. This can be formalized in regressions that show a significant reduction in surprises post - 2003, even after controlling for the ZLB. But beyond the very near term, it’s tough to find any discernible change; eyeballing the right -side chart you would be hard pressed to pick out a guidance-related shift in 2y UST reactions. This is also true for longer maturities (5y, 10y, 30y USTs) and even at horizons as short as the 2nd- quarter-ahead ED/SOFR futures contract. The inference we draw is that , while forward guidance and related communications have steered expectations for meetings towards delivered outcomes, it has not had a big impact in anchoring expectations beyond that. records.text: Alternate measures of job openings have receded in May and June (Figur es 6 and 7 ); consumer and small business surveys broadly point to stabilized labor demand rather than an acceleration; and we suspect that firmer wage growth will come as the job market tightens and inflation remains elevated. We look for the unemployment rate to fall to 4.0% in Q4, lower than the consensus 4.4% and a median Fed projection of 4.3%. Critically, our forecast does not require nonfarm payrolls to continuing matching the 188k average pace over the last three months. We look for 50- 75k monthly gains in H2, still enough to lower the unemployment rate by about 0.1pp/quarter given our breakeven estimate of 0-20k. The improved geopolitical backdrop leaves us more confident in this view , and even presents upside risks to our forecasts. Indeed, a persistent reduction in business uncertainty would increase the chance that activity is even stronger than projected in our above- consensus base case. Indeed, a sufficiently robust June payrolls print could prompt an earlier expected start date for Fed rate hikes, which we currently schedule in December (see US June FOMC: Every meeting is live, dated 18 June). We make some adjustments to our growth forecasts in the wake of PCE data released on 25 June and trade data on 26 June (Figure 8) – lower in Q2 at 2.5% annualized but up slightly in the out quarters, netting to a slightly stronger trajectory. records.text: 2022) shows that top-decile wealth shares tend to rise as real yields fall and bond prices increase, underscoring how monetary regimes shape distributional outcomes over time (Exhibit 13). Permanent wealth gains or temporary asset-price booms? A key question, however, is whether these asset-price gains are permanent or transitory. If rising asset values largely reflect stronger fundamentals and a durable increase in wealth, the resulting divergence may persist. If instead they reflect a temporary asset- price boom, the widening of the K may ultimately reverse as valuations normalize. Implications for monetary policy in the long run Since distinguishing between the two in real time is difficult, as in the case of AI driven strength in equity markets today, the Fed is unlikely to target the distributional consequences of asset-price movements directly and will instead focus on their implications for its dual mandate Policymakers will focus on whether asset-price movements pose risks to inflation, employment or financial stability. The strength in the PMI was driven by the services sector. Services having recently been more affected by weaker demand linked to the real-income shock from higher inflation. The fall in input costs is easing that shock, although a full recovery is likely to take time. Euro area consumer confidence, which is highly sensitive to inflation, improved in June, but by less than in May, and remains far from a full recovery. Manufacturing PMI eased in June, but the headline index is partly distorted by supplier delivery times (which do not handle well supply-side shocks). records.text: 26 June 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG Meanwhile, downstream, or bank-based, financial conditions have remained fairly robust, supporting economic activity. The next money and credit data (from which we derive the credit impulse – a leading indicator of private domestic demand) will be released on Monday, giving us the latest look at the downstream financial conditions. So far, lending flows and the credit impulse have remained fairly resilient. If these monthly flows continue at the level observed over the last three months, the credit impulse could improve further. Conversely, if bank lending flows prove marginal, the credit impulse may drop, although it is likely to remain positive. Despite the actual lending flows demonstrating resilience, there are warning signs ahead. The Q1-26 Bank Lending Survey (whose credit conditions are a leading indicator for the credit impulse) states banks are tightening credit standards amidst heightened risk, and demand is softening. This could potentially weigh on lending in the near future. Therefore, it will be crucial to assess whether monthly lending will slow over the next two months, or if the actual credit conditions reported in the upcoming Q2-26 Bank Lending Survey (scheduled for June 21st) turn out to be better than anticipated.
